Monetizing Intelligence:
Advertising and Subscription Design on LLM Platforms

Yuhang Ji1 Fasheng Xu2 Tianjun Feng1
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) platforms introducing advertising must decide how much capability ad revenue should fund and what consumers should pay to avoid ads. We study a monopolistic platform that jointly chooses costly response quality, advertising intensity, and subscription prices when advertising reduces user value but better service raises advertising returns. Three findings follow. First, when partly ad-supported and ad-free plans coexist, advertising can finance useful service for consumers who receive none under pure subscription. Lower effective quality in middle plans weakens the alternatives available to premium users, allowing higher prices for unchanged ad-free service. Some fully ad-supported users gain utility, while partly ad-supported and ad-free users lose: broader access can coexist with utility polarization. Second, an intermediate advertising cap can maximize consumer surplus by preserving some revenue that finances service while limiting degradation. Third, cheaper compute can raise quality and reduce ad intensity, yet sufficiently large cost reductions can increase aggregate advertising revenue above its initial level because better service raises the value of the remaining advertised interactions. An extension shows how advertising-funded upgrades can bring plans to the same maximum capability and advertising exposure, eliminating the basis for different prices. These results make menu design central to evaluating LLM advertising: the consequences extend beyond users who see ads to the alternatives and prices faced by those who do not.

keywords
Generative AI, LLM platforms, advertising, subscription design, mechanism design, consumer welfare

1 Introduction

An LLM platform that introduces advertising must decide how much capability to provide on its ad-supported plans and what users must pay to avoid ads. OpenAI’s February 2026 launch description makes this choice concrete: users could avoid ads by upgrading to Plus or Pro, or by accepting fewer daily messages on the Free tier (OpenAI 2026d). Advertising exposure, usage capacity, and subscription price are therefore linked choices. The financial stakes are substantial: on August 31, 2026, OpenAI reported that ChatGPT Ads had reached $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate (OpenAI 2026c). Microsoft’s Copilot-native ad formats and Meta’s use of AI interactions to personalize advertising illustrate other ways to monetize conversational activity (Sainsbury-Carter 2025, Meta 2025). For a platform offering both subscriptions and advertising, the central design problem is how to use ad revenue to fund service while preserving users’ incentives to pay for higher tiers.

Advertising can reduce the share of an LLM’s supplied capability that becomes useful assistance. For example, a sponsored product comparison may favor a product that fits the user’s needs less well, while concerns about commercial influence may weaken trust in the response. A recent experimental preprint finds that advertising disclosure attached to a product users explicitly seek reduces trust in the AI by lowering its perceived neutrality (Qin et al. 2026). Privacy concerns can also lead users to withhold context that the assistant needs to tailor its advice. Consistent with this concern, a survey finds that some AI-assistant users say they would become less willing to use personalization if advertising were introduced (Zappi 2026). These channels create a trade-off: advertising can help finance greater capability while reducing the value consumers obtain from it.

The same capability that makes an LLM useful to consumers can also make its advertising more valuable. In a product comparison, for example, a more capable model or greater inference effort can better interpret the user’s requirements and identify relevant alternatives, improving the information available for matching ads. Google reports using both the query and generated-answer content when serving ads in AI Overviews, while Microsoft describes using conversational signals to improve ad relevance (Google 2026, Sainsbury-Carter 2025). These practices motivate our focus on the advertising value of better service. Yet improving an ad-supported plan also gives premium users a more attractive alternative, potentially reducing what they will pay to avoid ads. The platform must therefore choose service quality, advertising exposure, and subscription prices together.

Advertising in AI assistants has already drawn legislative scrutiny. In 2026, U.S. Senator Edward Markey questioned seven major AI companies about advertising safeguards and introduced the Youth AI Privacy Act, which would ban chatbot advertising to minors (Markey 2026). We examine the economic trade-off behind restrictions on advertising through a cap on exposure: reducing commercial interference also restricts revenue that can make quality provision profitable. Because the platform can respond by changing quality and subscription prices, the cap’s benefit to consumers depends on how the entire menu adjusts. Technological progress changes these incentives from the cost side: inference prices have fallen sharply for models reaching comparable benchmark performance (Maslej 2025). As quality becomes cheaper to supply, platforms can improve service, reduce advertising, or combine the two. Better assistance can make advertising more valuable, but it also increases the value users lose when ads interfere with the service. We ask: How should an LLM platform combine advertising and subscriptions, and how do advertising limits and cheaper compute change its choices and consumers’ benefits?

We study a monopolistic LLM platform that commits to a menu of service plans, each specifying response quality, advertising intensity, and a subscription price. Consumers privately know how much they value quality and choose their preferred plan or leave the platform. Quality reflects the capability supplied through model choice, reasoning effort, or usage capacity, and improving it requires computational resources. The platform earns revenue from advertising exposure and an additional return when better service makes that advertising more valuable. Advertising also reduces the value consumers obtain from the service. Our analysis begins with a menu in which advertised and ad-free plans coexist and yields three main findings.

First, advertising can broaden access to useful service while leaving other consumers, including ad-free subscribers, worse off. Additional advertising revenue can make quality provision profitable for consumers who would receive no useful service under pure subscription, even after accounting for production costs and the potential loss of premium revenue when a better entry plan encourages users to switch down. We call this ad-funded quality democratization. Yet the benefit does not extend throughout the menu. When partially advertised and ad-free plans coexist, middle plans provide lower quality than under pure subscription: advertising reduces consumers’ willingness to pay for quality, and the added advertising return does not compensate for that loss. The weaker middle plans make premium subscribers less willing to switch down, allowing the platform to charge more for unchanged ad-free service. Some fully advertised users consequently gain, while users on partially advertised and ad-free plans lose utility relative to pure subscription, producing utility polarization.

Second, a moderate advertising cap can maximize consumers’ total surplus, yielding a better outcome than either unrestricted advertising or a complete ban. Limiting ads can make lower-tier plans more useful. When these plans become better alternatives to premium service, the platform must leave higher-valuation users more surplus to keep them from switching down. However, tighter limits also weaken the advertising return that encourages the platform to supply quality, and a complete ban removes this source of revenue. We identify settings in which consumers do best when advertising is limited enough to improve useful service but still allowed to help finance it.

Third, cheaper compute can support better service with less advertising, while advertising revenue can still rise. As quality becomes less costly, the platform supplies better service. For users on partially advertised plans, advertising then interferes with a more valuable service, inducing the platform to reduce exposure and extend ad-free access to more users. At the same time, better capability can raise the advertising value of users who continue to receive ads. With sufficiently large efficiency gains, the additional advertising value generated by fully advertised users who already receive useful service can outweigh revenue lost as other users see fewer ads, raising total advertising revenue above its initial level. This volume-to-value pivot shows why lower advertising exposure need not imply a smaller advertising business.

An extension shows how higher advertising returns to service quality can first expand the service menu and eventually lead tiers to merge. Initially, additional advertising revenue makes it profitable to offer useful service to the lowest-valuation consumers, creating a distinct quality tier. As returns rise further, however, advertising-funded upgrades can bring all groups to the same technological quality ceiling and full advertising exposure. Because consumers would choose the cheaper of otherwise identical plans, these tiers cannot sustain different prices and thus merge.

Our contribution is to explain how the dual role of produced quality shapes an advertising-supported subscription menu. Classic media models emphasize the trade-off between advertising nuisance and audience size (Anderson and Coate 2005, Peitz and Valletti 2008). Related screening work allows costly quality to influence advertising returns and, in a separate extension, allows advertising nuisance to depend on quality (Ichihashi et al. 2026); other work optimizes subscription fees and ad intensities with endogenous consumption (Gutt et al. 2026). Recent LLM-pricing models study compute allocation and access through token budgets or service caps (Bergemann et al. 2026, Zhong 2026). We bring both quality-dependent advertising forces into the platform’s joint choice of response quality for each consumer, advertising intensity, and price: better quality raises advertising returns, while advertising reduces the user value of that quality. The same quality choice therefore changes the value of the service to its intended consumer, the advertising revenue it generates, and the attractiveness of that plan to consumers elsewhere in the menu. Tracing these effects together connects quality provision at the bottom to the prices and utility of users above, including those who receive no advertising.

2 Literature Review

Our analysis connects three streams of work: monopoly screening and nonlinear pricing, the economics of ad-supported media platforms, and the emerging economics of AI platforms. We review each stream in turn and then position the paper against its closest antecedents.

The first stream is monopoly screening and nonlinear pricing. Mussa and Rosen (1978) study quality differentiation under private information, while Myerson (1981) develops the virtual-valuation approach to optimal mechanism design. Related work extends nonlinear pricing to multiproduct settings (Armstrong 1996), random participation (Rochet and Stole 2002), and information goods with negligible marginal cost (Sundararajan 2004). Two-sided platform theory explains how prices balance participation across market sides (Rochet and Tirole 2003); subsequent work studies second-degree price discrimination by two-sided monopoly platforms (Jeon et al. 2022) and screening through content access and advertising exposure (Ichihashi et al. 2026). Corrao et al. (2023) study nonlinear pricing when usage generates additional seller revenue and consumers may leave purchased services unused, with advertising among the applications. Alaei et al. (2023) optimize subscription bundles and fees for digital goods consumed by users with heterogeneous usage rates. Our analysis jointly chooses costly service quality and advertising exposure for each plan, with quality affecting both subscription payments and advertising revenue.

The second stream studies advertising-financed media, beginning with the trade-off between ad nuisance and content provision in broadcasting (Anderson and Coate 2005, Gabszewicz et al. 2004) and the comparison of advertising and subscription business models (Peitz and Valletti 2008); Anderson and Jullien (2015) survey this literature. Subsequent work examines ad targeting (Bergemann and Bonatti 2011), two-sided price discrimination by media platforms (Lin 2020), design biases in ad-funded markets (Choi and Jeon 2023), attention oligopoly (Prat and Valletti 2022), and how revenue models shape content moderation (Liu et al. 2022). Sato (2019) studies freemium as an optimal menu-pricing problem. These studies establish how advertising incentives interact with participation, content provision, and pricing. Our focus is quality produced for each consumer: allocating more capability changes the service delivered, the advertising returns it generates, and the attractiveness of that plan to users elsewhere in the menu. The closest-paper comparison below identifies how this joint design problem differs from existing quality and advertising extensions.

The third stream studies the economics of AI and LLM platforms. Empirical work documents differentiation and price dispersion among LLMs (Demirer et al. 2025), motivating models with endogenous service quality. Bergemann et al. (2026) derive token-budget menus from a homogeneous production technology, while Zhong (2026) studies screening through service caps when consumers differ in urgency; neither includes advertising. On the advertising side, Dütting et al. (2024) design token-level auctions for generated content, while Wang et al. (2025) study platform-controlled ad content and traffic across sequential sponsored-search positions. Alaei et al. (2026) study ad timing and advertiser selection as conversations reveal user preferences, designing mechanisms for privately informed advertisers. Zhang et al. (2026) choose whether to show ads on each query, balancing current advertising returns against future retention and subscription conversion. Our question concerns consumer screening through response quality, advertising intensity, and subscription prices when quality affects both advertising returns and the user value lost to advertising.

Empirical and computational evidence also documents commercial value in adjacent AI-mediated settings. Organic LLM referrals exhibit distinct e-commerce performance patterns (Kaiser and Schulze 2026), numerical experiments using field data show that LLM-assisted experimentation can improve content allocation (Ye et al. 2025), and GenAI-personalized video advertisements can increase engagement (Kapoor and Kumar 2025). These studies do not directly identify how raising the quality supplied to a consumer changes advertising returns; we therefore treat a positive quality-driven advertising premium as a modeling primitive motivated by the platform evidence summarized in Section 3.

Closely related studies examine complementary dimensions of this joint design problem. DeValve and Pekeč (2022) characterize subscription-price and advertising menus under monopoly and competition when consumers privately differ in advertising disutility. Our platform also chooses costly response quality, which affects advertising returns and the value consumers lose to advertising. Ichihashi et al. (2026) study screening through content access and advertising exposure, with broader access raising both advertising revenue and information rents. Their extensions allow costly item quality to increase advertising revenue and, separately, allow advertising nuisance to depend on item quality; these channels are used to study quality investment and item–ad matching, respectively. Gutt et al. (2026) optimize a continuous menu of ad intensities and subscription fees with endogenous user consumption, while holding content quality fixed. Their baseline fixes per-impression ad value; an extension lets it decline with ad load, rather than linking it to platform-produced response quality.

We study costly quality supplied to each consumer, jointly chosen with advertising intensity and price. Higher quality raises advertising returns, while advertising reduces the user value of that quality, so both channels enter the platform’s screening problem. Improving one plan therefore changes its revenue potential and its attractiveness as an alternative to other plans. The contribution is to trace these effects jointly through quality provision, information rents, and prices across the menu, including on plans that carry no advertising.

3 Model

We consider a monopolistic Large Language Model (LLM) platform serving a unit mass of consumers who differ in their valuation of response quality. The platform chooses the quality, advertising intensity, and subscription price of each plan, anticipating which plan each consumer will select. Higher quality is costly to produce, but it can support both subscription payments and advertising revenue. Advertising provides another source of revenue while reducing the effective quality consumers receive.

3.1 Consumers

Each consumer has a privately known type θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1], drawn from a cumulative distribution function FF with a continuous and strictly positive density ff on [0,1][0,1]. Type θ\theta is the consumer’s marginal valuation of effective response quality. Improving a lower-quality plan makes it more attractive to consumers who would otherwise pay for a higher-quality plan. To keep these consumers on the higher-quality plan, the platform may need to lower its price. Providing better service to one group can therefore reduce subscription revenue from another. Virtual value adjusts a consumer’s valuation for this indirect revenue cost and can be negative even when the consumer values the service. We impose the standard regularity condition that virtual value increases with type:11 1 The continuous-type model is a tractable baseline. Section 7 studies a discrete-type formulation and shows that advertising can non-monotonically change the number of positive-quality tiers.

{assumption}

The virtual value v⁡(θ)=θ−1−F⁡(θ)f⁡(θ)v(\theta)=\theta-\frac{1-F(\theta)}{f(\theta)} is strictly increasing and continuous.

Under this assumption, virtual value crosses zero at a unique type θ0∈(0,1)\theta_{0}\in(0,1). In the corresponding pure-subscription benchmark, the platform supplies no positive quality below this threshold: the screening cost outweighs the subscription return. Advertising can change that decision. If improving service also raises advertising revenue, the platform may profitably supply positive quality to some of these consumers and may also collect subscription payments.

3.2 Platform’s Instruments

The platform offers a menu of plans, {q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ),T⁡(θ)}θ∈[0,1]\{q(\theta),\alpha(\theta),T(\theta)\}_{\theta\in[0,1]}. Each plan specifies response quality, advertising intensity, and a subscription price. Here, q⁡(θ)≥0q(\theta)\geq 0 is a scalar index of the response capability supplied to type θ\theta. The platform can raise this index through model choice, inference effort, or usage capacity; these operational choices are summarized by the cost function introduced below. The subscription price is T⁡(θ)≥0T(\theta)\geq 0. Advertising intensity is α⁡(θ)∈[0,1]\alpha(\theta)\in[0,1]. At α=0\alpha=0, the consumer experiences no advertising-induced degradation; under the on-interface interpretation, the plan is ad-free. Positive values of α\alpha represent greater advertising intensity, up to the architectural limit α=1\alpha=1. Effective quality g⁡(q,α)g(q,\alpha) measures the service quality the consumer experiences after advertising-induced degradation.

OpenAI’s original February 2026 launch description illustrates the joint design of these instruments: users could avoid ads by upgrading to a paid plan or by opting out of ads in the Free tier in exchange for fewer daily free messages (OpenAI 2026d). This menu trades advertising exposure against either subscription payments or usage capacity, consistent with our interpretation of quality as including usage allowances.

Consumers benefit from supplied capability qq only when it produces assistance they can use and rely on. Advertising can reduce the share of this capability that becomes useful assistance through two channels. First, advertising can weaken the usefulness or credibility of a response. Consider a consumer asking an AI assistant to compare software products. If sponsorship steers the recommendation toward a product that fits the consumer’s needs less well, the same capability delivers less useful advice. Such output interference can arise through the selection, ranking, or framing of recommendations. Even when ads do not influence response content, as OpenAI states for ChatGPT (OpenAI 2026d), concerns about commercial influence may make the consumer less willing to rely on it. Evidence on perceived credibility comes from Qin et al. (2026), who find that advertising disclosure attached to a product users explicitly seek can reduce trust in the AI by lowering perceived neutrality.

Second, privacy friction can limit the information available to the assistant. For example, a business user seeking advice on improving a workflow may omit internal procedures or operational constraints out of concern that conversational data will be used for advertising. The assistant then has less context with which to tailor its advice, leaving some benefits of its capability unrealized. Context-based advertising makes this concern relevant: OpenAI uses conversational context to match ads, while Meta uses interactions with its AI features to personalize advertising across its apps (OpenAI 2026d, OpenAI 2026c, Meta 2025). Consistent with the possibility of reduced engagement, 27% of respondents in a survey of 1,000 U.S. AI-assistant users say they would become less willing to use personalization after advertising is introduced (Zappi 2026).

We assume that advertising-induced losses in effective quality are weakly larger at higher supplied quality, reflecting complementarity between capability, useful context, and consumer reliance. Losing a given fraction of useful assistance, for example, entails a larger absolute loss when the service has greater potential value.

3.3 Quality Production

The platform incurs computational costs when it generates responses for a consumer. Raising supplied quality qq can require a more capable model, more inference tokens, or a larger usage allowance on the same model. We summarize the cost of providing this service by c⁡(q)c(q) and impose the following conditions.

{assumption}

[Cost Function] The cost function c:ℝ+→ℝ+c:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} is twice continuously differentiable with c⁡(0)=0c(0)=0, c′​(0)=0c^{\prime}(0)=0, c′​(q)>0c^{\prime}(q)>0 for q>0q>0, c′′​(q)>0c^{\prime\prime}(q)>0, and limq→∞c′​(q)=∞\lim_{q\rightarrow\infty}c^{\prime}(q)=\infty.

Strict convexity means that each additional unit of quality costs more to provide. This assumption summarizes two ways the platform can improve service. First, routing users to more capable models can entail higher inference costs.22 2 Demirer et al. (2025) document a nonlinear relationship between model intelligence and API prices, with incremental intelligence improvements associated with larger price increases at the upper end. This pricing evidence motivates costly quality upgrading but does not identify the curvature of the platform’s production costs. Second, it can allocate more reasoning effort within a model. If additional inference yields progressively smaller quality gains, achieving a further quality improvement requires more computation. These considerations motivate convexity; they do not imply that every operational route to higher quality has the same cost curvature. We use continuous quality as a tractable approximation to model choice, inference effort, and usage capacity, consistent with standard vertical differentiation models (Mussa and Rosen 1978). Section 7 examines the core economic forces in a discrete-type formulation.

Quality is bounded by a technological ceiling, q≤q¯q\leq\bar{q}, representing limits on the capability the platform can supply. We set c′​(q¯)=1c^{\prime}(\bar{q})=1, so the ceiling equals the efficient quality for the highest-type consumer in an ad-free benchmark. This identity is a maintained link between production costs and feasible capability. Under the main specification and its regularity restrictions, the ceiling does not constrain quality for a positive mass of consumers. Section 6.2 allows the ceiling to expand as compute costs fall, while Section 7 examines tier pooling when it binds.

3.4 Consumer Utility

A type-θ\theta consumer assigned quality qq, advertising intensity α\alpha, and transfer TT obtains utility

U=θ​g​(q,α)−T,U=\theta g(q,\alpha)-T, (1)

where g⁡(q,α)g(q,\alpha) is the effective quality the consumer experiences after advertising-induced degradation. The single private type θ\theta determines both the value of this quality and the utility loss from reducing it. For a given plan with a positive advertising-induced quality loss, consumers who value quality more also lose more utility from that loss. The baseline has no separate dimension of private ad aversion. Output interference and privacy friction motivate the following restrictions on effective quality.

    gq​(q,α)>0g_{q}(q,\alpha)>0: Higher quality improves the user experience.

Condition (c) says that advertising weakly reduces the marginal value of supplied quality. Consequently, the effective-quality loss g⁡(q,0)−g⁡(q,α)g(q,0)-g(q,\alpha) is non-decreasing in qq for a fixed advertising intensity. The condition allows advertising to destroy more potential value when greater capability depends on trust or useful context. Because consumers differ in their valuation of effective quality, changing a plan’s ad load also changes its attractiveness relative to other plans. Advertising therefore enters both the platform’s revenue calculation and the incentive constraints governing plan choice.

3.5 Advertising Revenue

The platform earns advertising revenue R⁡(q,α)R(q,\alpha) from a consumer receiving supplied quality qq and advertising intensity α\alpha. We allow better service to make advertising more valuable by supporting richer interactions and more informative signals of commercial intent. This quality-driven ad premium gives the platform a return to quality in addition to subscription payments.

{assumption}

The advertising revenue function R:ℝ+×[0,1]→ℝ+R:\mathbb{R}_{+}\times[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} is twice continuously differentiable with R⁡(q,0)=0R(q,0)=0, Rα​(q,α)>0R_{\alpha}(q,\alpha)>0 for α<1\alpha<1, Rα​α​(q,α)<0R_{\alpha\alpha}(q,\alpha)<0, and Rq​(q,α)>0R_{q}(q,\alpha)>0 for α>0\alpha>0.

The condition Rα>0R_{\alpha}>0 for α<1\alpha<1 gives the platform a direct return to additional advertising, while Rα​α<0R_{\alpha\alpha}<0 imposes diminishing marginal returns. The condition Rq>0R_{q}>0 for α>0\alpha>0 means that better supplied quality increases the revenue from a given positive advertising intensity. For example, better matching can increase the probability that an ad is clicked; at a fixed payment per click, this raises expected revenue without increasing advertising exposure. Google reports that both the user query and the content of an AI Overview enter ad serving, while Microsoft attributes higher Copilot ad-relevance metrics to the richer signals contained in entire conversations (Google 2026, Sainsbury-Carter 2025). OpenAI similarly reports using conversational context to match advertisements and states that CPC and outcome-optimized bidding account for most campaigns (OpenAI 2026c). These practices motivate our assumption that better service raises advertising returns, although they do not directly establish this causal relationship.

With quality-linked advertising revenue, improving a plan changes both consumers’ willingness to pay and the advertising value of their interactions. Advertising-induced degradation (Assumption 3.4) and convex quality costs (Assumption 3.3) therefore enter the same design problem. Sections 4–7 examine how the platform balances these forces across the menu.
