Timing, Information, and Solution Concept.

The platform publicly posts and commits to its menu. Each consumer privately knows her type and selects a plan or the zero-utility outside option, participating when indifferent. The distribution FF and functions cc, RR, and gg are common knowledge. The platform then delivers the chosen allocation and collects payment, earning subscription and advertising revenue net of production cost. By the revelation principle, we represent the problem as a direct mechanism satisfying (3) and (4). Full commitment is maintained; Appendix B.1 discusses its role.

Aggregate consumer surplus is C​S:=∫01[θ​g​(q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ))−T⁡(θ)]​𝑑F​(θ)CS:=\int_{0}^{1}[\theta g(q(\theta),\alpha(\theta))-T(\theta)]\,dF(\theta). We define social welfare, S​WSW, as consumer surplus plus the platform’s expected profit in (2). This measure includes the platform’s advertising revenue; it does not separately account for advertiser surplus.

3.7 Main Specification

For an explicit characterization of the optimal menu, we use a uniform type distribution, θ∼U⁡[0,1]\theta\sim U[0,1]. Then f⁡(θ)=1f(\theta)=1, virtual value is v⁡(θ)=2​θ−1v(\theta)=2\theta-1, and the virtual-zero type is θ0=1/2\theta_{0}=1/2. Computational cost is quadratic, c⁡(q)=β​q2/2c(q)=\beta q^{2}/2, where β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1] is the compute-cost parameter. Lower β\beta means that any given quality costs less to provide. The maintained ceiling condition c′​(q¯)=1c^{\prime}(\bar{q})=1 then gives q¯=1/β\bar{q}=1/\beta. The baseline normalizes β=1\beta=1 and hence q¯=1\bar{q}=1; Section 6.2 studies lower compute costs together with the implied expansion of the quality ceiling.

We capture the interaction between quality and advertising with a multiplicative function:

g⁡(q,α)=q⁡(1−δ​α),g(q,\alpha)=q(1-\delta\alpha), (5)

where δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) measures the proportional quality loss per unit of advertising intensity. Consumers experience full supplied quality qq when α=0\alpha=0 and retain q⁡(1−δ)q(1-\delta) when α=1\alpha=1. Thus, a fixed positive ad load removes the same fraction of supplied quality at every qq, but a larger absolute amount when supplied quality is higher. This reduced-form loss represents the output-interference and privacy-friction channels described in Section 3.2, without modeling either channel separately.

Finally, the advertising revenue is specified as:

R⁡(q,α)=λ​q​α+r¯​(α−α22),R(q,\alpha)=\lambda q\alpha+\bar{r}\left(\alpha-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\right), (6)

Here, λ>0\lambda>0 measures the advertising return to supplied quality: at a fixed positive ad load, higher qq raises the quality-linked component λ​q​α\lambda q\alpha. The parameter r¯>0\bar{r}>0 governs the quality-independent component, which has diminishing returns to advertising intensity and remains available at q=0q=0. At q=0q=0, baseline revenue comes from impressions generated by consumers who participate in a minimal-capability ad-supported layer. Consumers assigned q=T=0q=T=0 obtain zero utility and participate under the indifference convention stated above. This specification satisfies Assumption 3.5.

A larger quality-driven premium λ\lambda can make positive quality profitable for consumers who receive none under pure subscription. Greater degradation δ\delta lowers the intended consumer’s willingness to pay but also makes the plan less attractive to higher-valuation consumers. This can reduce the utility the platform must leave higher types to discourage them from choosing plans intended for lower types. This utility, which arises because consumers’ valuations are private, is their information rent. Baseline ad profitability r¯\bar{r} adds a quality-independent return, including at the zero-quality baseline. Section 4 combines these effects to determine quality and advertising across the menu.

To ensure an endogenous ad-free premium tier, we impose the following parameter restrictions.

{assumption}

[Market Regularity] δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), λ∈(0,δ)\lambda\in(0,\delta), and r¯∈(0,δ−λ)\bar{r}\in(0,\delta-\lambda).

The bounds on λ\lambda and r¯\bar{r} in Assumption 3.7 keep advertising profitability low enough for an ad-free premium segment (e.g., ChatGPT Plus/Pro) to coexist with ad-supported segments. Appendix C.1 characterizes the remaining parameter regions and their implications, with even the highest type receiving advertising when λ+r¯>δ\lambda+\bar{r}>\delta. Under the baseline normalization β=1\beta=1, these restrictions also ensure that the quality ceiling does not bind for a positive mass of consumers.

Appendix B.1 discusses the roles of the functional forms, one-dimensional private information, full commitment, and monopoly. It also explains the consumer- and platform-side extensions, the limits of the reduced-form competition diagnostic, and the applicability of the framework beyond LLM platforms.

4 Optimal Mechanism

The platform must decide how much quality advertising can profitably support and which consumers should be offered ad-free service. At a given positive quality, more advertising brings revenue but weakens the plan’s appeal to consumers who value quality, including premium users who could switch down. Upgrading the plan instead raises its advertising return while making it a stronger alternative to premium service. The return to either decision therefore includes its effect on subscription revenue elsewhere in the menu. We use virtual-surplus maximization to combine these effects and derive the segmented menu in Theorem 4.5.

4.1 Reduction to Virtual Surplus

Let U⁡(θ):=θ​g​(q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ))−T⁡(θ)U(\theta):=\theta g(q(\theta),\alpha(\theta))-T(\theta) denote type θ\theta’s equilibrium utility. Incentive compatibility links the utility offered to each type to the effective quality available to lower types. This link determines transfers up to the lowest type’s utility and allows us to express the platform’s problem in terms of quality and advertising alone.

Lemma 4.1 (Virtual Surplus Representation)

The platform’s problem has the following representation:

  1. (a)(a)

    Incentive compatibility. In any incentive-compatible mechanism, U⁡(θ)U(\theta) is absolutely continuous with U′​(θ)=g⁡(q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ))U^{\prime}(\theta)=g(q(\theta),\alpha(\theta)) almost everywhere, and effective quality g⁡(q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ))g(q(\theta),\alpha(\theta)) is non-decreasing in θ\theta.

  2. (b)(b)

    Profit representation. Individual rationality and nonnegative payments imply U⁡(0)=0U(0)=0. The platform’s problem is therefore equivalent to maximizing expected virtual surplus:

    max⁡∫01q⁡(⋅),α⁡(⋅)⁡𝒱⁡(θ,q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ))​𝑑F​(θ)\max_{q(\cdot),\alpha(\cdot)}\int_{0}^{1}\mathcal{V}(\theta;q(\theta),\alpha(\theta))dF(\theta) (7)

    subject to the original allocation bounds and the requirement that g⁡(q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ))g(q(\theta),\alpha(\theta)) be non-decreasing in θ\theta, where

    𝒱⁡(θ,q,α):=v⁡(θ)​g​(q,α)⏟Virtual Quality Value+R⁡(q,α)⏟Ad Revenue−c⁡(q)⏟Quality Cost,\mathcal{V}(\theta;q,\alpha):=\underbrace{v(\theta)g(q,\alpha)}_{\text{Virtual Quality Value}}+\underbrace{R(q,\alpha)}_{\text{Ad Revenue}}-\underbrace{c(q)}_{\text{Quality Cost}}, (8)

    and v⁡(θ)=θ−1−F⁡(θ)f⁡(θ)v(\theta)=\theta-\frac{1-F(\theta)}{f(\theta)} is the virtual value.

Part (a) expresses each subscription payment as the consumer’s gross value of service less the utility required for incentive compatibility:

T⁡(θ)=θ⋅g⁡(q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ))−U⁡(0)−∫0θg⁡(q⁡(t),α⁡(t))​𝑑t.T(\theta)=\theta\cdot g(q(\theta),\alpha(\theta))-U(0)-\int_{0}^{\theta}g(q(t),\alpha(t))dt. (9)

The lowest type has U⁡(0)=−T⁡(0)U(0)=-T(0), so individual rationality and T⁡(0)≥0T(0)\geq 0 force U⁡(0)=T⁡(0)=0U(0)=T(0)=0. The integral is therefore the consumer’s information rent, which increases with the effective quality available to lower types. Because U′​(θ)=g⁡(q⁡(θ),α⁡(θ))≥0U^{\prime}(\theta)=g(q(\theta),\alpha(\theta))\geq 0, higher types also satisfy individual rationality. Substituting (9) into the objective and integrating by parts yields part (b).

4.2 Virtual Advertising Profit

To isolate the advertising trade-off, decompose the pointwise virtual surplus into a pure-subscription baseline and an advertising-driven component:

𝒱⁡(θ,q,α)=v⁡(θ)​g​(q,0)−c⁡(q)⏟Pure Subscription Surplus+R⁡(q,α)−v⁡(θ)​(g⁡(q,0)−g⁡(q,α))⏟Virtual Advertising Profit,\mathcal{V}(\theta;q,\alpha)=\underbrace{v(\theta)g(q,0)-c(q)}_{\text{Pure Subscription Surplus}}+\underbrace{R(q,\alpha)-v(\theta)(g(q,0)-g(q,\alpha))}_{\text{Virtual Advertising Profit}}, (10)

where g⁡(q,0)−g⁡(q,α)≥0g(q,0)-g(q,\alpha)\geq 0 captures the effective-quality loss from advertising.

Definition 4.2 (Virtual Advertising Profit)

For type θ\theta, define

ρθ​(α,q):=R⁡(q,α)−v⁡(θ)​(g⁡(q,0)−g⁡(q,α)).\rho_{\theta}(\alpha;q):=R(q,\alpha)-v(\theta)(g(q,0)-g(q,\alpha)). (11)

Virtual advertising profit measures the change in the platform’s virtual surplus from adding advertising at fixed quality. Expanding v⁡(θ)=θ−1−F⁡(θ)f⁡(θ)v(\theta)=\theta-\frac{1-F(\theta)}{f(\theta)} separates three effects. The platform earns advertising revenue R⁡(q,α)R(q,\alpha), but the effective-quality loss lowers type θ\theta’s willingness to pay by θ⁡(g⁡(q,0)−g⁡(q,α))\theta\bigl(g(q,0)-g(q,\alpha)\bigr). At the same time, making this allocation less attractive to higher types reduces the information rents the platform must leave them, yielding the offsetting term 1−F⁡(θ)f⁡(θ)​(g⁡(q,0)−g⁡(q,α))\frac{1-F(\theta)}{f(\theta)}\bigl(g(q,0)-g(q,\alpha)\bigr). The last two effects combine into −v⁡(θ)​(g⁡(q,0)−g⁡(q,α))-v(\theta)\bigl(g(q,0)-g(q,\alpha)\bigr). For non-positive virtual values, the rent savings weakly outweigh the loss in willingness to pay, so degradation does not reduce virtual surplus. For positive virtual values, willingness-to-pay losses dominate, creating a net cost that is weakly increasing in quality under Assumption 3.4(c). This difference helps explain why advertising can fund quality for low types while inducing the platform to limit advertising on higher tiers.

4.3 Pointwise Optimization

We now use the baseline specification in Section 3.7 and maintain Assumption 3.7 throughout the subsequent analysis, unless otherwise stated. In the pure-subscription benchmark (α≡0\alpha\equiv 0), maximizing virtual surplus yields qs​u​b​(θ)=max⁡{0,2​θ−1}q^{sub}(\theta)=\max\{0,2\theta-1\}: types θ≤1/2\theta\leq 1/2 receive zero quality, while higher types receive positive quality. This allocation provides the benchmark for identifying the quality changes induced by advertising. We first solve the hybrid problem type by type while retaining the allocation bounds and temporarily ignoring the requirement that effective quality be non-decreasing in type.33 3 Under our specification, effective quality g⁡(q∗,α∗)g(q^{*},\alpha^{*}) is non-decreasing (and strictly increasing wherever q∗​(θ)>0q^{*}(\theta)>0), as verified in the proof of Theorem 4.5; non-monotonic alternatives would require standard ironing (Myerson 1981).

Virtual advertising profit is ρθ​(α,q)=λ​q​α+r¯​(α−α22)−(2​θ−1)​q​δ​α\rho_{\theta}(\alpha;q)=\lambda q\alpha+\bar{r}(\alpha-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2})-(2\theta-1)q\delta\alpha. Maximizing the full pointwise virtual surplus in (8), including subscription value and production cost, gives the quality choice conditional on advertising intensity:

q∗​(θ,α)=max⁡{0,(2​θ−1)​(1−δ​α)+λ​α}.q^{*}(\theta,\alpha)=\max\{0,(2\theta-1)(1-\delta\alpha)+\lambda\alpha\}. (12)

The term λ​α\lambda\alpha adds an advertising return to supplied quality, while −(2​θ−1)​δ​α-(2\theta-1)\delta\alpha captures the change in its virtual value caused by degradation. For negative virtual values, the latter term is positive because degradation reduces the information rents associated with providing quality to lower types.

For fixed quality, the platform adds advertising as long as marginal ad revenue exceeds the net degradation cost:

∂ρθ∂α=λ​q+r¯​(1−α)⏟Marginal Ad Revenue−(2​θ−1)​q​δ⏟Net Degradation Cost.\frac{\partial\rho_{\theta}}{\partial\alpha}=\underbrace{\lambda q+\bar{r}(1-\alpha)}_{\text{Marginal Ad Revenue}}-\underbrace{(2\theta-1)q\delta}_{\text{Net Degradation Cost}}. (13)

Consider first consumers with non-positive virtual type, θ≤1/2\theta\leq 1/2. For these consumers, the rent savings from ad-induced degradation weakly outweigh the loss in willingness to pay. Together with direct advertising revenue, this makes the maximal ad load optimal. Positive quality requires an additional incentive: the quality-driven ad premium λ\lambda must be large enough to offset the negative marginal virtual value of serving these consumers.

Proposition 4.3 (Advertising-Funded Quality)

For every θ∈[0,1/2]\theta\in[0,1/2], the optimal advertising intensity is α∗​(θ)=1\alpha^{*}(\theta)=1, and the optimal quality is q∗​(θ)=max⁡{0,(2​θ−1)​(1−δ)+λ}q^{*}(\theta)=\max\{0,(2\theta-1)(1-\delta)+\lambda\}. In particular, every type θ<1/2\theta<1/2 satisfying (2​θ−1)​(1−δ)+λ>0(2\theta-1)(1-\delta)+\lambda>0 receives strictly positive quality despite having a negative virtual value.

Proposition 4.3 separates the incentive to show advertising from the incentive to supply positive quality. Baseline ad profitability (r¯>0\bar{r}>0) supports the maximal ad load for θ≤1/2\theta\leq 1/2, even when quality is zero. Supplying positive quality to negative-virtual-value consumers requires the quality-driven premium: because Rq=λ​α>0R_{q}=\lambda\alpha>0, improving their service also increases advertising revenue. In the counterfactual with λ=0\lambda=0, advertising revenue is independent of quality, the positive-quality threshold returns to θ¯=1/2\underline{\theta}=1/2, and q∗​(θ)=max⁡{0,(2​θ−1)​(1−δ)}=0q^{*}(\theta)=\max\{0,(2\theta-1)(1-\delta)\}=0 for all θ<1/2\theta<1/2. Conversely, in the boundary counterfactual r¯=0\bar{r}=0, a positive λ\lambda can still support positive quality for some consumers with negative virtual values. Appendix A.5 replaces λ​q​α\lambda q\alpha with λ​h​(q)​α\lambda h(q)\alpha and shows that advertising can still induce q∗​(θ)>0q^{*}(\theta)>0 for some consumers with negative virtual values.

Consumers with positive virtual type (θ>1/2\theta>1/2) all receive positive quality. For fixed qq, ∂𝒱/∂α=r¯​(1−α)−q​Δ​(θ)\partial\mathcal{V}/\partial\alpha=\bar{r}(1-\alpha)-q\Delta(\theta), where Δ⁡(θ):=(2​θ−1)​δ−λ\Delta(\theta):=(2\theta-1)\delta-\lambda. Here, q​Δ​(θ)q\Delta(\theta) measures the marginal cost of advertising to the platform, after accounting for the quality-driven ad return. The platform retains the full advertising load when Δ⁡(θ)≤0\Delta(\theta)\leq 0. As θ\theta rises, Δ⁡(θ)\Delta(\theta) increases. When Δ⁡(θ)>0\Delta(\theta)>0, the platform reduces advertising, with the following interior solutions whenever the optimal ad load remains positive:44 4 See Appendix D.2 for the derivations of (12) and (14).

αi​n​t​(θ)=r¯−(2​θ−1)​Δ​(θ)r¯−Δ​(θ)2,qi​n​t​(θ)=r¯​((2​θ−1)−Δ⁡(θ))r¯−Δ​(θ)2.\alpha^{int}(\theta)=\frac{\bar{r}-(2\theta-1)\Delta(\theta)}{\bar{r}-\Delta(\theta)^{2}},\hskip 10.00002ptq^{int}(\theta)=\frac{\bar{r}((2\theta-1)-\Delta(\theta))}{\bar{r}-\Delta(\theta)^{2}}. (14)

For the highest types, the marginal gain from adding advertising at their optimal ad-free quality q=2​θ−1q=2\theta-1 is non-positive, so the platform sets α∗=0\alpha^{*}=0. Theorem 4.5 combines these choices with Proposition 4.3 to characterize the optimal menu.

4.4 Characterization of the Optimal Mechanism

The pointwise choices form a menu with three distinct boundaries: where positive quality begins, where the platform starts reducing the ad load, and where it removes advertising.

Definition 4.4 (Critical Thresholds)

Define the following thresholds:

  1. (1)

    Positive-quality threshold: θ¯:=12−λ2​(1−δ)\underline{\theta}:=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{2(1-\delta)}, above which consumer types receive positive quality.

  2. (2)

    Partial-ad threshold: θ1:=12+λ2​δ\theta_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2\delta}, above which the platform reduces the ad load below one.

  3. (3)

    Ad-free threshold: θ2∈(θ1,1)\theta_{2}\in(\theta_{1},1) uniquely solving (2​θ2−1)​[(2​θ2−1)​δ−λ]=r¯(2\theta_{2}-1)[(2\theta_{2}-1)\delta-\lambda]=\bar{r}, equivalently θ2=2​δ+λ+λ2+4​δ​r¯4​δ\theta_{2}=\frac{2\delta+\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+4\delta\bar{r}}}{4\delta}, at and above which the platform eliminates advertising.

Using these thresholds, the optimal allocations are summarized as follows.

Theorem 4.5 (Optimal Mechanism)

The optimal mechanism partitions the market into up to four segments:

  1. (a)(a)

    Zero-quality baseline (θ∈[0,θ¯]\theta\in[0,\underline{\theta}], empty when θ¯<0\underline{\theta}<0): consumers receive q∗​(θ)=0q^{*}(\theta)=0, α∗​(θ)=1\alpha^{*}(\theta)=1, and T∗​(θ)=0T^{*}(\theta)=0.

  2. (b)(b)

    Positive quality with full advertising (low types) (θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1] with θ¯<θ≤θ1\underline{\theta}<\theta\leq\theta_{1}): consumers receive q∗​(θ)=(2​θ−1)​(1−δ)+λ>0q^{*}(\theta)=(2\theta-1)(1-\delta)+\lambda>0 and α∗​(θ)=1\alpha^{*}(\theta)=1. Payments satisfy T∗​(θ)>0T^{*}(\theta)>0 for θ>0\theta>0, with T∗​(0)=0T^{*}(0)=0 when θ¯<0\underline{\theta}<0.

  3. (c)(c)

    Partial advertising (medium types) (θ∈(θ1,θ2)\theta\in(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})): consumers receive q∗​(θ)=qi​n​t​(θ)q^{*}(\theta)=q^{int}(\theta) and α∗​(θ)=αi​n​t​(θ)∈(0,1)\alpha^{*}(\theta)=\alpha^{int}(\theta)\in(0,1), as defined in (14).

  4. (d)(d)

    Ad-free service (high types) (θ≥θ2\theta\geq\theta_{2}): consumers receive the pure-subscription monopoly quality q∗​(θ)=2​θ−1q^{*}(\theta)=2\theta-1, face no advertising (α∗​(θ)=0\alpha^{*}(\theta)=0), and pay the highest subscription prices on the menu.

Payments are recovered from (9) with U⁡(0)=0U(0)=0. Effective quality g⁡(q∗​(θ),α∗​(θ))g(q^{*}(\theta),\alpha^{*}(\theta)) is non-decreasing in type and strictly increasing wherever q∗​(θ)>0q^{*}(\theta)>0, so the pointwise allocations are implementable without ironing.

Relative to pure subscription, the optimal menu raises supplied quality on positive-quality, fully advertised plans below θ1\theta_{1}. Here, the quality-driven advertising return exceeds the virtual cost of degradation, so improving service is more profitable than under pure subscription. This return can support positive quality for some consumers who would receive zero quality under pure subscription; fully advertised positive-quality plans can also carry subscription charges. For middle types, some advertising remains profitable, but the degradation it causes lowers the net return to improving service, so the platform supplies less quality than under pure subscription. The advertising return and virtual degradation cost balance at θ1\theta_{1}, while supplied quality also matches the benchmark for ad-free consumers and consumers who continue to receive zero quality. Evaluating who benefits additionally requires tracing subscription payments and information rents across the menu.

OpenAI’s Go launch announcement paired higher usage allowances and longer memory than Free with planned advertising in Free and Go and ad-free Plus and Pro tiers (OpenAI 2026b, OpenAI 2026d). These choices illustrate the separate roles of supplied capability and advertising exposure; they do not establish the predicted quality distortions relative to pure subscription.

Remark 4.6 (Zero-Quality Baseline)

The allocation (q∗,α∗,T∗)=(0,1,0)(q^{*},\alpha^{*},T^{*})=(0,1,0) represents the limiting case of a minimal-capability, ad-supported layer. Zero quality means zero effective service quality; consumers obtain zero utility and participate under the maintained indifference convention, allowing the platform to earn baseline advertising revenue R⁡(0,1)=r¯/2R(0,1)=\bar{r}/2. Within the regular parameter region, this segment has positive mass when λ<1−δ\lambda<1-\delta. At λ=1−δ\lambda=1-\delta, only the lowest type receives zero quality; when λ>1−δ\lambda>1-\delta, the quality-driven advertising return supports positive quality for every type. Appendix B.2 tabulates the menu within this region, and Appendix C.1 analyzes the broader parameter regions.

5 How Advertising Reshapes Quality, Prices, and Welfare

Evaluating advertising requires tracking both the service consumers receive and what they pay after the platform redesigns its menu. We first ask whether greater harm from advertising necessarily reduces supplied capability, and then whether more profitable impressions lower subscription prices (Sections 5.1 and 5.2). These are parameter changes within the hybrid model. Section 5.3 instead compares the optimized hybrid menu with pure subscription to determine which users benefit, separating individual utility from aggregate consumer surplus and social welfare.

5.1 Quality Responses to Ad Degradation (δ\delta)

We first increase ad degradation δ\delta, holding the advertising-revenue parameters fixed. On a positive-quality plan carrying advertising, greater degradation reduces effective service at a fixed supplied quality and ad load. The platform can respond by changing both quality and advertising, so this direct loss does not determine the direction of its quality choice. Proposition 5.1 identifies the resulting local responses and the expansion of positive-quality provision when a zero-quality segment exists. Figure 1 illustrates how quality and advertising move together at the stated parameter values; its curves compare finite changes, whereas the proposition distinguishes local responses within the relevant regions.

Proposition 5.1 (Quality Distortion)

A marginal increase in δ\delta, holding λ\lambda and r¯\bar{r} fixed and remaining in the regular region, changes supplied quality as follows:

  1. (a)(a)

    Entry into positive quality: The threshold θ¯\underline{\theta} decreases. When it lies inside the type support, consumers between the new and old cutoffs gain positive quality, while those below the new cutoff remain at zero.

  2. (b)(b)

    Positive-quality low types (α∗=1\alpha^{*}=1): For feasible types θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1] with θ¯<θ≤θ1\underline{\theta}<\theta\leq\theta_{1}, quality increases if θ<1/2\theta<1/2, is unchanged if θ=1/2\theta=1/2, and decreases if θ>1/2\theta>1/2.

  3. (c)(c)

    Medium types (αi​n​t∈(0,1)\alpha^{int}\in(0,1)): Locally within this segment, quality decreases under a heavy ad load (αi​n​t>1/2\alpha^{int}>1/2), is unchanged to first order at αi​n​t=1/2\alpha^{int}=1/2, and increases under a light ad load (αi​n​t<1/2\alpha^{int}<1/2).

  4. (d)(d)

    High types (α∗=0\alpha^{*}=0): Quality remains unchanged at 2​θ−12\theta-1 for consumers who remain ad-free.

All increases and decreases in parts (b) and (c) are strict. At moving segment boundaries, the comparison concerns an increase in δ\delta, rather than asserting two-sided differentiability.

For fully advertised users below the median valuation, greater degradation makes their plans less attractive to higher types who might switch down. The resulting rent savings lower the screening cost of supplying quality at the bottom. Because the quality-driven premium λ\lambda rewards that quality, the platform raises supplied quality for these users whenever it is already positive and expands positive-quality provision when the cutoff lies inside the type support. This response requires λ>0\lambda>0: with quality-independent advertising (λ=0\lambda=0), below-median users continue to receive zero quality, as in Proposition 4.3. An increase in supplied quality is not itself a claim that effective quality or consumer utility rises.

For users above the median, greater degradation reduces the virtual return to quality at any fixed positive ad load. For users who locally remain fully advertised, ad intensity stays at one, so the direct effect lowers supplied quality. For medium types, reducing advertising can offset this direct effect: fewer ads expose less of the supplied capability to degradation and thereby raise the return to quality. The precise cutoff follows from the baseline functional forms: at an interior optimum, the advertising condition is qi​n​t​Δ=r¯​(1−αi​n​t)q^{int}\Delta=\bar{r}(1-\alpha^{int}). Combining this condition with the quality choice makes the local quality response proportional to (1−αi​n​t)−αi​n​t(1-\alpha^{int})-\alpha^{int}, with a positive multiplier. Under a light ad load, the optimal reduction in advertising therefore more than offsets the direct loss, so quality rises. Under a heavy ad load, the adjustment in advertising does not offset the direct loss, so quality falls; at an ad load of one-half, the effects exactly balance to first order. For consumers who remain ad-free, degradation affects neither their allocation nor supplied quality.

The empirical prediction concerns supplied capability as well as advertising exposure. Holding the other primitives fixed, greater degradation widens the supplied-quality gap between heavily advertised medium types who locally remain in that segment and users who remain ad-free. Supplied quality can vary through usage caps, context limits, model routing, or feature access, so access to a newer model alone does not measure this gap. Testing the prediction would require identifying a degradation change and accounting for concurrent changes in capabilities and costs; observing an upgraded entry plan alone does not establish the model’s incentive.

5.2 Divergent Pricing: Baseline Ad Profitability (r¯\bar{r})

A higher return to impressions improves the revenue available from a given advertised plan, but does not determine how subscription prices change across the menu. Consumers who pay to avoid advertising can therefore be affected even when their own service is unchanged. We isolate this response by increasing baseline ad profitability r¯\bar{r}, the quality-independent return to impressions, while holding λ\lambda and δ\delta fixed and allowing quality and advertising to adjust. OpenAI’s impression-based advertising option illustrates the billing unit (OpenAI 2026a); separating this return from the quality-driven premium is a modeling assumption.

A higher r¯\bar{r} makes advertising more profitable, weakly raising ad intensity and weakly lowering supplied and effective quality across the market, as illustrated in Figure 2(a). Yet lower effective quality need not reduce every subscription price: the same menu adjustment changes the information rents required to keep higher types on their plans. Proposition 5.2 distinguishes users who locally remain in each segment.

Proposition 5.2 (Divergent Pricing)

Consider a marginal increase in r¯\bar{r}, holding λ\lambda and δ\delta fixed and remaining in the regular region. For a fixed consumer type away from the segment thresholds:

  1. (a)(a)

    Zero-quality and low types (α∗=1\alpha^{*}=1): The subscription price is unchanged.

  2. (b)(b)

    Medium types (αi​n​t∈(0,1)\alpha^{int}\in(0,1)): The subscription price strictly decreases.

  3. (c)(c)

    High types (α∗=0\alpha^{*}=0): The subscription price strictly increases despite unchanged quality and advertising.

The price equals gross utility minus the information rent left to the consumer: T∗​(θ)=θ⋅g⁡(q∗​(θ),α∗​(θ))−U⁡(θ)T^{*}(\theta)=\theta\cdot g(q^{*}(\theta),\alpha^{*}(\theta))-U(\theta). Fully advertised plans carry the maximal ad load, and a higher r¯\bar{r} adds no marginal return to quality, so their allocations and those below them remain unchanged. Both gross utility and information rent therefore stay fixed, leaving their prices unchanged. For medium types, a higher r¯\bar{r} lowers both effective quality and information rents. The effective-quality loss becomes larger at higher types within this segment, making each user’s loss in gross utility exceed the reduction in her information rent; her incentive-compatible price therefore falls. For users who remain ad-free, gross utility is unchanged, but the deterioration of lower tiers makes downward switching less attractive and reduces the information rent needed to keep them on their assigned tier. The platform can therefore charge these users more for the same allocation.

The empirical counterpart is a change in the return to impressions, such as an identified CPM shock, holding compute costs, platform capabilities, and market structure fixed (OpenAI 2026a). For users who remain in their segments, the model predicts lower prices on partially advertised plans and higher prices on unchanged ad-free plans. Quality and advertising are allowed to adjust; only segment membership must remain locally unchanged. A change in the incremental advertising return to quality instead maps to λ\lambda, and a change in compute costs maps to β\beta. Observed prices and CPMs may reflect several of these forces, as well as competition and menu-adjustment costs, so their co-movement alone does not isolate the predicted cross-tier price divergence.

5.3 Consumer Utility and Aggregate Welfare

We now compare the optimized hybrid menu with the pure-subscription benchmark to ask which consumers gain after quality, advertising, and payments all adjust. The hybrid menu has a positive quality-driven ad premium λ\lambda: supplying better service can make interactions more valuable for advertising. Google’s use of queries and AI Overview content in ad serving, Microsoft’s use of conversational signals for ad relevance, and Meta’s announced use of AI interactions to personalize advertising illustrate the role of interaction content (Google 2026, Sainsbury-Carter 2025, Meta 2025). They motivate the channel without establishing the marginal return to supplied quality or calibrating λ\lambda.

Figure 3 compares supplied quality and consumer utility with their pure-subscription levels. The ad-free quality curves coincide at the top in panel (a), yet the utility curves remain separated in panel (b): a consumer’s unchanged allocation does not guarantee unchanged utility when the rest of the menu changes. Proposition 5.3 establishes which consumers gain or lose throughout the regular parameter region.

Proposition 5.3 (Utility Polarization)

Compare the optimal hybrid menu with λ>0\lambda>0 to the pure-subscription benchmark:

  1. (a)(a)

    Positive-quality low types (α∗=1\alpha^{*}=1): If λ≤1−δ\lambda\leq 1-\delta, every type θ∈(max⁡{0,θ¯},θ1)\theta\in(\max\{0,\underline{\theta}\},\theta_{1}) strictly gains utility, and utility equals the benchmark at θ1\theta_{1}. If λ>1−δ\lambda>1-\delta, only a subset of these types strictly gains, and utility at θ1\theta_{1} is strictly below the benchmark.

  2. (b)(b)

    Medium and high types: Every type in the partial-ad segment (αi​n​t∈(0,1)\alpha^{int}\in(0,1)) and the ad-free segment (α∗=0\alpha^{*}=0) strictly loses utility.

Consumers who receive zero quality, and type θ=0\theta=0, have unchanged zero utility.

The utility comparison depends on effective quality along the menu, not supplied quality alone. By the envelope condition, each type’s information rent accumulates the effective quality offered below it. On the fully advertised segment, this gives U⁡(θ)=([q∗​(θ)]2−[q∗​(0)]2)/4U(\theta)=\bigl([q^{*}(\theta)]^{2}-[q^{*}(0)]^{2}\bigr)/4. When λ≤1−δ\lambda\leq 1-\delta, the lowest type receives zero quality, so q∗​(0)=0q^{*}(0)=0. The higher supplied quality of positive-quality low types below θ1\theta_{1} therefore translates into higher utility; at θ1\theta_{1}, their quality matches the subscription benchmark and the utility gain vanishes. When λ>1−δ\lambda>1-\delta, however, even the lowest type receives positive quality, q∗​(0)=λ+δ−1q^{*}(0)=\lambda+\delta-1, while still obtaining zero utility. The rent formula must therefore subtract the positive term [q∗​(0)]2/4[q^{*}(0)]^{2}/4. Because supplied quality matches the benchmark at θ1\theta_{1}, this subtraction makes hybrid utility strictly lower there, leaving only a subset of positive-quality low types better off.

Above θ1\theta_{1}, medium types receive lower effective quality than in the benchmark, so their utility increases more slowly with type and every medium type loses. The ad-free top retains its benchmark allocation but inherits the lower information rent accumulated below it, allowing the platform to charge more for the same service. Thus, advertising affects even consumers who see no ads through the quality and pricing of the alternatives available to them.

Strict convexity of quality costs supports the smooth, type-dependent quality choices in the baseline, but Remark B.1 in Appendix B.2 explains why polarization need not require this cost shape. With linear costs and an independently fixed finite technological ceiling, quality becomes a boundary choice rather than a smoothly varying allocation. Advertising and information-rent effects can still generate utility polarization in that setting.

Welfare Implications.

Aggregate consumer surplus adds the utility gains and losses identified in Proposition 5.3. It rises when the integrated gains at the bottom exceed the losses above, falls when the losses exceed the gains, and is unchanged when they balance. Social welfare is defined here as consumer surplus plus platform profit: subscription payments cancel in this sum, while the value of effective service, advertising revenue, and quality costs remain. In particular, ad-free consumers receive the same allocation as under pure subscription, so their utility losses are entirely higher payments that transfer surplus to the platform. The remaining welfare comparison weighs advertising revenue and additional service at the bottom against changes in effective service and production costs on advertised plans. The proof of Proposition 5.3 establishes that this balance is strictly positive throughout the regular region, so hybrid monetization raises social welfare even when aggregate consumer surplus falls. It also establishes that social welfare strictly increases with λ\lambda, holding δ\delta and r¯\bar{r} fixed and remaining in that region.

These comparisons take platform operation as given. The compute-cost projections motivating the paper (Reuters 2026) raise a separate viability question: if fixed infrastructure costs made pure subscription unprofitable, its optimized menu might not be an attainable market alternative. Exit or other adjustments would then require additional analysis; the present polarization result compares consumer utility with the pure-subscription optimum and does not establish the comparison with platform exit.

Product and policy assessments therefore need to consider the distribution of gains across the menu as well as the capability of the entry plan. An upgraded ad-supported plan can coexist with utility losses elsewhere, and higher social welfare can coexist with lower aggregate consumer surplus. Table 2 in Appendix B.2 summarizes the segment-level results. The next section asks when limits on advertising or lower quality costs can improve consumer outcomes while preserving the service that advertising helps finance.

6 Advertising Caps and Compute Efficiency

Two practical decisions follow from the preceding analysis: how tightly to limit advertising to protect consumers, and how a platform should redesign its menu when quality becomes cheaper to supply. At a given supplied quality, reducing advertising improves the user experience; the value of a cap also depends on the quality and prices the platform offers in response. Cheaper compute changes the return to upgrading service and can also change which plans should carry advertising. Both decisions must account for the alternatives available elsewhere in the menu, because changes to advertised plans affect the surplus left to premium users.

The advertising cap analysis retains β=1\beta=1; the compute-efficiency analysis relaxes this normalization and allows the technological ceiling to expand as specified below.

6.1 Advertising Caps and Consumer Surplus (α¯\bar{\alpha})

A platform introducing advertising into a conversational interface must decide how much commercial influence to allow while preserving users’ trust in its responses. OpenAI and Microsoft state that sponsored content should remain distinct from, and should not influence, organic responses (OpenAI 2026d, Sainsbury-Carter 2025). Disclosure may not resolve the concern: users can fail to recognize sponsored recommendations embedded in chatbot responses even when disclosure is provided (Tang et al. 2025). Policy scrutiny now directly targets advertising in AI assistants. In 2026, U.S. Senator Edward Markey questioned seven major AI companies about advertising safeguards and introduced the Youth AI Privacy Act, which would ban chatbot advertising to minors (Markey 2026). We study the service-quality and pricing consequences of restricting advertising exposure by imposing an intensity cap, α⁡(θ)≤α¯∈[0,1]\alpha(\theta)\leq\bar{\alpha}\in[0,1]. The cap lets us compare a complete ban with partial limits and unrestricted advertising while allowing the platform to redesign its menu. Disclosure and separation policies can also affect how much a given ad load degrades user value; Section 5.1 studies changes in this second margin through δ\delta.

If quality provision were fixed, reducing advertising would improve the quality consumers experience. The platform, however, redesigns its menu when a cap restricts the advertising revenue that helps fund quality. A tighter cap therefore reduces advertising-induced degradation while weakening the return to ad-subsidized quality provision. Figure 4(a) illustrates how these opposing effects can make consumer surplus (C​SCS) non-monotonic in α¯\bar{\alpha} at (δ,λ,r¯)=(0.9,0.5,0.18)(\delta,\lambda,\bar{r})=(0.9,0.5,0.18). Holding λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 and r¯=0.18\bar{r}=0.18, Panel (b) shows where a cap improves consumer surplus relative to the unregulated benchmark: the blue region satisfies C​S​(α¯)>C​S​(1)CS(\bar{\alpha})>CS(1), includes sufficiently mild caps throughout the plotted range of δ\delta, and extends to strict caps at higher degradation levels. This comparison describes a particular parameter slice. Proposition 6.1 separates a local condition for improvement from the existence of primitives for which every maximizing cap is interior.

Proposition 6.1 (Interior-Cap Optimum)

Let C​S​(α¯)CS(\bar{\alpha}) denote aggregate consumer surplus under the cap α⁡(θ)≤α¯\alpha(\theta)\leq\bar{\alpha}.

  1. (a)(a)

    Local improvement: If δ>5/8\delta>5/8 and λ>λ^local​(δ)\lambda>\hat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{local}}(\delta), where λ^local​(δ)\hat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{local}}(\delta) is given in closed form in the proof, then marginally tightening the unregulated benchmark α¯=1\bar{\alpha}=1 strictly raises consumer surplus. Hence α¯=1\bar{\alpha}=1 is not consumer-surplus maximizing.

  2. (b)(b)

    Interior optimality in a nonempty region: The set of primitives for which every consumer-surplus-maximizing cap lies in (0,1)(0,1) is nonempty. At (δ,λ,r¯)=(0.9, 0.5, 0.18)(\delta,\lambda,\bar{r})=(0.9,\,0.5,\,0.18), direct evaluation of the exact constrained allocation gives C​S​(0.78)≈0.04898>C​S​(0)≈0.04167>C​S​(1)≈0.03155CS(0.78)\approx 0.04898>CS(0)\approx 0.04167>CS(1)\approx 0.03155. Hence every maximizing cap is strictly interior at this instance, and the same conclusion holds in a neighborhood of these primitives.

A tighter cap trades less degradation against weaker quality funding, and changes in lower-tier effective quality alter the information rents passed to users above them. Proposition 6.1(a) gives sufficient conditions for the degradation reduction to dominate locally. This local gain does not by itself establish an interior optimum; part (b) establishes that stronger conclusion for a nonempty set of primitives. The opposite local effect arises whenever a zero-quality segment exists (λ<1−δ\lambda<1-\delta): marginally tightening the unregulated cap strictly reduces consumer surplus. Here, a tighter cap weakens ad funding and raises the cutoff for positive quality, so some marginal consumers lose effective service; under the maintained specification, the loss from reduced ad-funded quality dominates locally. The following numerical example illustrates how these forces can instead favor a moderate cap, with the allocation and rent responses shown in Figure 5 in Appendix B.2.

In the illustrated economy, first tighten the cap from α¯=1\bar{\alpha}=1 toward the consumer-surplus peak α¯∗\bar{\alpha}^{*}. Severe ad degradation initially leaves low tiers with little effective quality (Figure 5(a)), making them unattractive alternatives for higher-value users and allowing the platform to leave those users less information rent. A moderate cap reduces advertising-induced degradation, so some lower tiers can offer higher effective quality even as their supplied quality qq falls. As these alternatives become more attractive, the platform must leave higher types more utility to keep them on their intended plans (Figure 5(b)). Over this range of caps, the resulting gains on balance raise aggregate consumer surplus.

Tightening the cap further can reverse this gain. In the illustrated economy, consumer surplus falls as the cap moves below α¯∗\bar{\alpha}^{*} toward the low-cap trough α¯L\bar{\alpha}^{L} in Figure 4(a). A tighter cap reduces the advertising return earned on each unit of quality, so the platform cuts quality provision below the median valuation; by the trough, most of these users receive zero quality. Their lower effective quality also reduces the information rents passed to users above them through the incentive-compatible menu. For users in the original partial-ad middle whose advertising choices the cap now constrains, both supplied quality and effective quality rise as the cap tightens. Between the peak and the trough, however, these improvements are insufficient to offset the loss of ad-funded quality at the bottom, and aggregate consumer surplus falls.

In the illustrated economy, further tightening from α¯L\bar{\alpha}^{L} toward a complete ban (α¯=0\bar{\alpha}=0) raises aggregate consumer surplus again. By the trough, most below-median users have already lost positive-quality service, leaving little ad-subsidized quality at the bottom to sacrifice as the cap tightens further. The ban eliminates advertising revenue and restores pure-subscription screening. It removes the remaining ad-subsidized quality below the median, but it also removes advertising-induced degradation and raises supplied quality for users in the original partial-ad middle. The higher effective quality offered to these middle users increases the information rents their allocations generate for users above them. In this instance, the resulting consumer-surplus gain outweighs the loss of the remaining quality at the bottom, so the ban delivers more consumer surplus than the trough. An intermediate cap nevertheless performs better than the ban: as Proposition 6.1 establishes for this instance and a neighborhood of its primitives, preserving some ad-subsidized quality while limiting its degradation yields a strictly interior consumer-surplus optimum.

A cap restricts the platform’s choices and cannot raise its maximized profit, so a consumer-surplus gain need not raise social welfare. Appendix C.2 identifies a narrow possibility from marginally tightening the unregulated benchmark, requiring sufficiently severe degradation and an intermediate range of quality-driven advertising premiums.

6.2 Compute Efficiency, Service Quality, and Advertising (β\beta)

Cheaper compute gives a platform a choice about how to redesign its menu: supply more capability, reduce advertising, or combine the two. These adjustments pull advertising revenue in different directions. Better service makes advertising more valuable, but it also gives consumers more useful capability to lose through advertising-induced degradation. The platform must balance these effects when deciding which plans to upgrade and which should carry fewer ads. We examine the resulting allocations and payoffs, and then ask whether reduced exposure necessarily means less advertising revenue.

Model distillation, more efficient routing, and hardware acceleration can reduce the compute required to deliver a given capability. These improvements correspond to a lower β\beta in c⁡(q)=β​q2/2c(q)=\beta q^{2}/2. Following Appendix C.3, we hold (δ,λ,r¯)(\delta,\lambda,\bar{r}) fixed and vary β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1]; the maintained technological ceiling expands with efficiency because q¯=1/β\bar{q}=1/\beta. The advertising regions retain their structure: the positive-quality threshold θ¯\underline{\theta} and ad-saturation threshold θ1\theta_{1} remain fixed, while the ad-free threshold becomes θ2,β=2​δ+λ+λ2+4​δ​β​r¯4​δ\theta_{2,\beta}=\frac{2\delta+\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+4\delta\beta\bar{r}}}{4\delta}. As β\beta falls, this upper boundary moves left, so more consumers receive ad-free service and allocations change within the remaining regions.

Proposition 6.2 (Effects of Improved Compute Efficiency)

Improved compute efficiency (β↓\beta\downarrow) has the following effects:

  1. (a)(a)

    Allocations: Optimal quality weakly increases and advertising intensity weakly decreases for every consumer type.

  2. (b)(b)

    Payoffs: Each consumer type’s utility and the platform’s profit weakly increase.

  3. (c)(c)

    Segment membership: The ad-free premium segment expands.

Proposition 6.2 identifies a tier-specific response to cheaper quality. Positive-quality users on fully advertised plans receive more capability while their ad load remains unchanged. In the partial-ad middle, the platform both raises quality and reduces advertising: degradation imposes a positive net cost after accounting for quality-linked advertising revenue, and raising quality increases this cost. Once the net cost of even the first increment of advertising exceeds its baseline advertising return, a plan becomes ad-free. Thus, cheaper compute can lead the platform to remove advertising from more plans even though better service also makes advertising more valuable. The resulting increase in effective quality weakly raises every type’s utility through the incentive-compatible rent schedule. Platform profit also weakly rises: the old menu remains incentive compatible and individually rational, fits within the expanded ceiling, and costs less to supply. The platform therefore improves the consumer experience without having to sacrifice profit to do so.

Less advertising per user and a larger ad-free segment both put downward pressure on advertising revenue. Does this mean that cheaper compute weakens the advertising business? Proposition 6.3 shows why the quality of the remaining ad-supported interactions also matters.

Proposition 6.3 (The Volume-to-Value Pivot)

Improved compute efficiency weakly reduces advertising intensity for every user. Nevertheless, letting Rt​o​t​a​l​(β)R_{total}(\beta) denote aggregate advertising revenue under compute-cost parameter β\beta, there exists β^∈(0,1)\hat{\beta}\in(0,1) such that Rt​o​t​a​l​(β^)>Rt​o​t​a​l​(1)R_{total}(\hat{\beta})>R_{total}(1): aggregate advertising revenue can exceed its level at the baseline β=1\beta=1.

The platform earns advertising revenue from both the intensity of advertising and the quality of the interactions in which it appears. Cheaper compute weakly lowers advertising intensity and moves some middle types into the ad-free segment, reducing revenue through the volume channel. Higher quality raises the quality-driven advertising return at a given ad intensity; for middle types who continue to receive ads, total advertising revenue rises only if this gain outweighs the lower intensity. The fully ad-saturated, positive-quality low-type segment provides a sharper comparison because its mass and advertising intensity (α∗=1\alpha^{*}=1) do not depend on β\beta. Quality in this segment is proportional to 1/β1/\beta, so its quality-linked advertising revenue grows at the same rate. Under the linear premium λ​q​α\lambda q\alpha and expanding ceiling q¯=1/β\bar{q}=1/\beta, this segment’s advertising revenue becomes arbitrarily large as β\beta approaches zero. It therefore eventually offsets revenue lost as other users receive fewer ads, establishing the comparison with the finite baseline revenue in Proposition 6.3.55 5 This comparison with β=1\beta=1 does not imply that advertising revenue rises after every marginal cost reduction.

Appendix A.5 examines whether this gain survives diminishing advertising returns to quality. Under its stated conditions, the comparison between two fixed cost levels remains valid for concave premiums sufficiently close to the linear benchmark. A separate numerical example with bounded, diminishing advertising returns to quality shows that reducing β\beta from 11 to 0.50.5 raises aggregate advertising revenue by about 3.6%3.6\% while weakly reducing advertising intensity for every type. Thus, the increase need not rely on unbounded advertising value, although it is not guaranteed for arbitrary concave premiums. For a platform assessing its revenue outlook, the implication is to track the quality and advertising value of remaining advertised service alongside ad intensity and the share of ad-free users.

The compute-efficiency analysis shows how cheaper quality changes capability and advertising across a continuous menu. The next section asks a different design question: whether stronger advertising returns lead the platform to offer more distinct positive-quality tiers or to combine existing tiers. It holds quality costs and the technological ceiling fixed while increasing the advertising return to quality, isolating the effect of monetization on the scope for service differentiation.

7 An Extension: When Service Tiers Converge

Advertising-funded upgrading can do more than widen access: it can erode the differences on which subscription prices depend. This extension asks when stronger advertising returns make separate contracts cease to be optimal because consumer groups receive the same quality and advertising exposure. Unlike the compute-efficiency analysis, we hold quality costs and the technological ceiling fixed while increasing the quality-driven ad premium λ\lambda. A moderate premium can finance entry into positive quality, whereas stronger returns can push groups to the same allocation. We count distinct positive-quality contracts, excluding the zero-quality baseline in Remark 4.6. In the three-type framework below, Proposition 7.1 establishes a 22–33–22–11 sequence in the number of positive-quality tiers.

We replace the continuous type distribution with equally sized Low (LL), Middle (MM), and High (HH) groups, with θL=0\theta_{L}=0, θM∈(1/2,1)\theta_{M}\in(1/2,1), and θH=1\theta_{H}=1. The model retains the baseline cost and revenue functions with β=1\beta=1, q¯=1\bar{q}=1, and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), but relaxes Assumption 3.7 to include parameter regions without an ad-free premium segment. The virtual valuations are vL=−2​θM<0v_{L}=-2\theta_{M}<0, vM=2​θM−1>0v_{M}=2\theta_{M}-1>0, and vH=1v_{H}=1. Pure subscription supplies qualities vMv_{M} and vHv_{H} to the upper groups and zero quality to LL. At a full ad load, unconstrained quality is q~i​(1)=(1−δ)​vi+λ\tilde{q}_{i}(1)=(1-\delta)v_{i}+\lambda, which rises with the premium for every group. The three thresholds below mark its becoming positive for LL, reaching the ceiling for MM, and reaching the ceiling for LL; their ordering places entry before upper-type pooling. The platform must compare interior candidates with boundary allocations, because the ceiling eventually binds. Appendix D.13 provides the discrete calculation and stationary candidates, with exact allocations in Table 3.

Proposition 7.1 (Expansion-then-Pooling of Service Tiers)

In our three-type framework, define the thresholds for type LL to receive positive quality, upper-type pooling, and universal pooling as λL:=2​θM​(1−δ)\lambda_{L}:=2\theta_{M}(1-\delta), λM:=q¯−(2​θM−1)​(1−δ)\lambda_{M}:=\bar{q}-(2\theta_{M}-1)(1-\delta), and λU:=q¯+2​θM​(1−δ)\lambda_{U}:=\bar{q}+2\theta_{M}(1-\delta). Suppose 0<r¯≤δ−λL0<\bar{r}\leq\delta-\lambda_{L}, which implies λL<λM<λU\lambda_{L}<\lambda_{M}<\lambda_{U}. The optimal menu has:

  1. (a)(a)

    Ad initiation, λ∈(0,λL]\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{L}]: Two positive-quality tiers, serving MM and HH separately.

  2. (b)(b)

    Full separation, λ∈(λL,λM)\lambda\in(\lambda_{L},\lambda_{M}): Three distinct positive-quality tiers, one for each group.

  3. (c)(c)

    Top pooling, λ∈[λM,λU)\lambda\in[\lambda_{M},\lambda_{U}): Two positive-quality tiers, with MM and HH sharing a plan and LL remaining separate.

  4. (d)(d)

    Universal pooling, λ≥λU\lambda\geq\lambda_{U}: One positive-quality tier shared by all three groups.

Initially, improving the low group’s free baseline would earn more advertising revenue but also make downward switching more attractive to paying consumers, increasing the information rents needed to retain them. The negative virtual valuation vLv_{L} captures this screening cost, which a small quality-driven premium cannot cover. Type LL therefore remains at the fully advertised zero-quality baseline, while MM and HH receive positive quality. The high group remains ad-free under the stated restrictions. If the middle plan carries an interior ad load, its quality-driven advertising return does not yet offset the virtual cost of degradation, so it supplies less quality than under pure subscription. Once λ\lambda exceeds λL\lambda_{L}, advertising revenue justifies upgrading the low group into a third positive-quality tier. This tier is free and fully advertised: the normalization θL=0\theta_{L}=0 leaves no subscription willingness to pay, while the advertiser-side return supports quality provision. The expansion upgrades an existing layer and need not add a newly listed plan. Advertising can subsequently reach the high group while all three allocations remain distinct; the detailed ad-load transitions are reported in Table 3.

At λM\lambda_{M}, type MM reaches the quality ceiling already attained by HH. At these premiums, the quality-driven advertising return exceeds the virtual cost of degradation even for HH, so both upper groups receive the full ad load. Identical quality and advertising require the same price, leaving two positive-quality contracts. During top pooling, upgrading the low plan makes it a better alternative for upper types, so their unchanged common plan must become cheaper. At λU\lambda_{U}, the low group also reaches the ceiling, and every group receives (q∗,α∗)=(q¯,1)(q^{*},\alpha^{*})=(\bar{q},1). The normalization θL=0\theta_{L}=0 makes this common plan free, leaving advertising as the revenue source. The fixed ceiling is essential: without it, full-ad qualities remain strictly ordered and this pooling mechanism disappears.

For a platform upgrading an ad-supported offering, the practical question is whether capability differences and differences in ad exposure still support separate subscription prices. The model concerns distinct positive-quality contracts; attributes and plan-management costs outside the benchmark can still support different marketed plans. Universal pooling requires the strong advertising return specified by λU\lambda_{U}, above the highest consumer-side valuation under q¯=θH=1\bar{q}=\theta_{H}=1; reliance on advertising revenue alone does not establish this condition. OpenAI’s Free, Go, Plus, and Pro offerings illustrate a granular menu, while Meta AI combines a free core service with paid bundles offering higher usage of compute-intensive AI features (Meta 2026). These examples establish the relevance of choosing differentiated offerings, but do not show that advertising causes them to converge. Evidence for the mechanism would need to connect stronger quality-driven advertising returns to narrower capability differences, converging ad exposure, and the disappearance of associated price differences, while accounting for compute constraints and scarcity, bundling, competition, and legacy ecosystem effects.

Beyond tier counts, the preceding analysis suggests three additional tests of the quality, screening, and compute-efficiency mechanisms. First, examine whether better service raises advertising revenue per interaction, holding ad exposure, user intent, and advertiser conditions comparable. Second, tracking capability allowances, subscription prices, advertising exposure, and users’ tier switching together could test the predicted screening responses across the menu. Third, decomposing advertising-revenue growth into user growth, ad frequency, advertiser demand, and revenue per impression could help distinguish exposure-driven growth from the quality-linked value channel in the compute-efficiency result.

8 Conclusion

An LLM platform’s joint choice of quality, advertising, and prices affects the entire subscription menu, including users who never see an ad. When partly ad-supported and ad-free plans coexist, advertising can finance useful service for consumers who receive none under pure subscription, but middle plans deliver less effective quality than under pure subscription, allowing the platform to charge more for unchanged premium service. Some fully ad-supported users gain utility, while partly ad-supported and ad-free users lose. This utility polarization means that broader access can coexist with greater rent extraction from existing subscribers.

Advertising caps should therefore be assessed through their effects on service quality and prices, as well as exposure. A moderate cap can improve lower-tier service and strengthen premium users’ alternatives while preserving revenue that supports quality. Tighter limits can remove the return that sustains quality at the bottom. In some settings, a moderate cap yields more consumer surplus than either a ban or unrestricted advertising. The welfare objective remains distinct: a cap cannot raise maximized platform profit, and gains to consumers need not raise total welfare. Disclosure and separation rules may instead change how exposure degrades assistance and require a different comparison.

Cheaper compute supports better service with fewer ads and broader ad-free access, leaving consumers and the platform at least as well off. With sufficiently large efficiency gains, higher advertising value from fully advertised users already receiving useful service can outweigh reduced exposure elsewhere and lift aggregate advertising revenue above its initial level. This volume-to-value pivot makes delivered capability important alongside ad counts.

The findings concern a monopolistic platform that can commit to its menu and consumers who differ in their valuation of quality. In the tier extension, strong advertising returns can bring plans to the same maximum capability and exposure, eliminating price differences supported by those attributes; other forms of differentiation remain possible. The e-companion examines alternative user-value and advertising-return specifications, with conclusions specific to each environment. Its competition diagnostic preserves a local pattern of opposite price responses across partly ad-supported and ad-free users, but does not determine how competitors set and revise posted prices.

Future work could endogenize the feedbacks that this framework holds fixed. If commercial influence weakens trust and context sharing, the loss of future advertising value may discipline current ad loads. Linking advertiser demand and auction design (Dütting et al. 2024) to consumer screening could clarify when thin advertiser markets weaken ad-funded access. External influence through Generative Engine Optimization or data poisoning, and revenue tied to completed purchases, raise further questions about whether monetization improves matching or intensifies steering.

Appendix A Model Extensions

These extensions examine which parts of the baseline mechanism depend on its specification. Additive nuisance changes the lowest allocation because the platform must keep effective quality nonnegative; type-dependent and concave advertising premiums change the returns to serving different consumers. Direct ad utility yields an allocation equivalence after adjusting the effective advertising premium. The correlated-degradation and competition exercises are diagnostics with more limited interpretations. Throughout, we distinguish restrictions that preserve the allocation structure from the smaller neighborhoods in which comparative statics and utility comparisons persist.

A.1 Mixed Ad Degradation

Our baseline analysis focuses on quality-dependent proportional ad degradation (δ\delta), a feature central to generative AI platforms. We now allow ads to generate an additional quality-independent nuisance component (δn\delta_{n}), such as visual interruptions or other disruptions that do not scale with service quality. To examine the robustness of our main results, we extend the effective quality function to incorporate both effects:

g⁡(q,α)=q⁡(1−δ​α)−δn​α,g(q,\alpha)=q(1-\delta\alpha)-\delta_{n}\alpha, (15)

where δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) captures multiplicative degradation and δn≥0\delta_{n}\geq 0 captures additive nuisance. We maintain θ∼U⁡[0,1]\theta\sim U[0,1], v⁡(θ)=2​θ−1v(\theta)=2\theta-1, c⁡(q)=q2/2c(q)=q^{2}/2, and R⁡(q,α)=λ​q​α+r¯​(α−α2/2)R(q,\alpha)=\lambda q\alpha+\bar{r}(\alpha-\alpha^{2}/2). Consistent with Assumption 3.4, the feasible set in this extension explicitly requires g⁡(q,α)≥0g(q,\alpha)\geq 0. We impose λ∈(0,δ)\lambda\in(0,\delta) and r¯∈(0,δ−λ)\bar{r}\in(0,\delta-\lambda). To state the exact structural restriction, define

εB:=λ⁡(1−δ)​(2−δ),εH:={+∞,r¯≥λ2,r¯+δ​r¯λ−r¯,0<r¯<λ2,εS:=min⁡{εB,εH}.\varepsilon_{B}:=\lambda(1-\delta)(2-\delta),\hskip 18.49988pt\varepsilon_{H}:=\begin{cases}+\infty,&\bar{r}\geq\lambda^{2},\\[3.0pt] \displaystyle\sqrt{\bar{r}}+\frac{\delta\bar{r}}{\lambda-\sqrt{\bar{r}}},&0<\bar{r}<\lambda^{2},\end{cases}\hskip 18.49988pt\varepsilon_{S}:=\min\{\varepsilon_{B},\varepsilon_{H}\}.

The bound εB\varepsilon_{B} keeps the zero-effective-quality boundary and the adjacent full-ad segment distinct, whereas εH\varepsilon_{H} preserves the ordering of the full-ad/interior and interior/ad-free thresholds and the interior second-order condition.

Let Δm​(θ):=δ⁡(2​θ−1)−λ\Delta_{m}(\theta):=\delta(2\theta-1)-\lambda. Define the interior allocations as

αmi​n​t​(θ)=r¯−(2​θ−1)​[Δm​(θ)+δn]r¯−Δm​(θ)2,qmi​n​t​(θ)=r¯​[(2​θ−1)−Δm​(θ)]+(2​θ−1)​δn​Δm​(θ)r¯−Δm​(θ)2.\alpha_{m}^{int}(\theta)=\frac{\bar{r}-(2\theta-1)[\Delta_{m}(\theta)+\delta_{n}]}{\bar{r}-\Delta_{m}(\theta)^{2}},\hskip 18.49988ptq_{m}^{int}(\theta)=\frac{\bar{r}[(2\theta-1)-\Delta_{m}(\theta)]+(2\theta-1)\delta_{n}\Delta_{m}(\theta)}{\bar{r}-\Delta_{m}(\theta)^{2}}.

θ¯m=12−λ2​(1−δ)+δn2​(1−δ)2,\underline{\theta}^{m}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{2(1-\delta)}+\frac{\delta_{n}}{2(1-\delta)^{2}},

while θ1m\theta_{1}^{m} and θ2m\theta_{2}^{m} are defined by

[λ+(2​θ1m−1)​(1−δ)]​[λ−δ⁡(2​θ1m−1)]=δn​(2​θ1m−1),(2​θ2m−1)​[Δm​(θ2m)+δn]=r¯.\bigl[\lambda+(2\theta_{1}^{m}-1)(1-\delta)\bigr]\bigl[\lambda-\delta(2\theta_{1}^{m}-1)\bigr]=\delta_{n}(2\theta_{1}^{m}-1),\hskip 18.49988pt(2\theta_{2}^{m}-1)\bigl[\Delta_{m}(\theta_{2}^{m})+\delta_{n}\bigr]=\bar{r}.
Theorem A.1 (Optimal Mechanism under Mixed Ad Degradation)

Under (15) and δn∈[0,εS)\delta_{n}\in[0,\varepsilon_{S}), the optimal mechanism takes the following four-segment form when θ¯m>0\underline{\theta}^{m}>0:

  1. (a)(a)

    Bottom types θ∈[0,θ¯m]\theta\in[0,\underline{\theta}^{m}]: q∗​(θ)=δn1−δq^{*}(\theta)=\frac{\delta_{n}}{1-\delta}, α∗​(θ)=1\alpha^{*}(\theta)=1, and g⁡(q∗​(θ),α∗​(θ))=0g(q^{*}(\theta),\alpha^{*}(\theta))=0.

  2. (b)(b)

    Low types θ∈(θ¯m,θ1m]\theta\in(\underline{\theta}^{m},\theta_{1}^{m}]: q∗​(θ)=(2​θ−1)​(1−δ)+λq^{*}(\theta)=(2\theta-1)(1-\delta)+\lambda and α∗​(θ)=1\alpha^{*}(\theta)=1.

  3. (c)(c)

    Medium types θ∈(θ1m,θ2m]\theta\in(\theta_{1}^{m},\theta_{2}^{m}]: q∗​(θ)=qmi​n​t​(θ)q^{*}(\theta)=q_{m}^{int}(\theta) and α∗​(θ)=αmi​n​t​(θ)\alpha^{*}(\theta)=\alpha_{m}^{int}(\theta).

  4. (d)(d)

    High types θ≥θ2m\theta\geq\theta_{2}^{m}: q∗​(θ)=2​θ−1q^{*}(\theta)=2\theta-1 and α∗​(θ)=0\alpha^{*}(\theta)=0.

Additive nuisance changes what the platform must provide at the bottom. When the lowest segment exists, full advertising requires produced quality δn/(1−δ)\delta_{n}/(1-\delta) merely to offset the nuisance, leaving these consumers with zero effective quality. Thus the bottom allocation can use costly capability even though it supplies no net user value. Under δn<εS\delta_{n}<\varepsilon_{S}, both this boundary pool and the adjacent positive-effective-quality segment remain fully ad-supported. The additional condition δn<λ⁡(1−δ)\delta_{n}<\lambda(1-\delta) places the boundary threshold below the median type, θ¯m<1/2\underline{\theta}^{m}<1/2; it is an interpretive restriction rather than the maximal restriction supporting the four-segment structure.

Proposition A.2 (Local Robustness under Mixed Ad Degradation)

Fix (δ,λ,r¯)(\delta,\lambda,\bar{r}) satisfying the mixed analogue of Assumption 3.7. There exists δ¯n∈(0,min⁡{εS,λ⁡(1−δ)/2})\bar{\delta}_{n}\in\bigl(0,\min\{\varepsilon_{S},\lambda(1-\delta)/2\}\bigr) such that, for every δn∈[0,δ¯n)\delta_{n}\in[0,\bar{\delta}_{n}):

  1. (a)(a)

    Quality. As δ\delta rises, the positive-effective-quality threshold moves left. Within the positive-effective-quality full-ad segment, quality rises below the median and falls above it; the baseline interior-quality signs persist on compact subsets away from the sign-switching locus.

  2. (b)(b)

    Prices. The divergent interior- and ad-free-price signs with respect to r¯\bar{r} persist on compact subsets away from thresholds.

  3. (c)(c)

    Utility. There exist nonempty compact low- and high-type intervals on which the utility gain and loss, respectively, relative to pure subscription persist.

The theorem characterizes allocations throughout the stated structural range, whereas the proposition preserves the baseline comparative statics only for sufficiently small additive nuisance. The distinction matters because maintaining the order of the segments does not by itself preserve every derivative or utility comparison. The local argument uses the strict baseline signs on the specified compact sets, which survive a sufficiently small perturbation. The proofs are provided in Appendices D.14 and D.15.

A.2 Correlated Ad Degradation: A Diagnostic

The baseline model assumes a homogeneous ad-degradation parameter. We now consider a diagnostic specification in which users with higher willingness to pay for AI quality are also more likely to be sensitive to ad-induced distortion, as may be the case for professional or enterprise users who place greater weight on reliability, neutrality, and privacy. The interpretation differs across the two advertising channels introduced in Section 3.2. Under on-interface advertising, response interference can make users who value quality and neutrality more exposed to degradation; the December 2025 controversy over ad-like app suggestions shown to some paying ChatGPT subscribers illustrates this concern (Ha 2025). Under off-interface advertising, privacy sensitivity may instead be distinct from quality valuation, so positive correlation should be understood as a diagnostic benchmark rather than a general restriction. To capture this idea, suppose that, conditional on θ∼U⁡[0,1]\theta\sim U[0,1], the consumer is in a high-degradation state with probability θ\theta and in a low-degradation state with probability 1−θ1-\theta:

δH=2​δ​with probability ​θ,δL=δ​with probability ​1−θ.\delta_{H}=2\delta\hskip 9.24994pt\text{with probability }\theta,\hskip 18.49988pt\delta_{L}=\delta\hskip 9.24994pt\text{with probability }1-\theta.

We impose δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2), together with λ∈(0,δ)\lambda\in(0,\delta) and r¯∈(0,δ−λ)\bar{r}\in(0,\delta-\lambda), so that both degradation states remain within the admissible range of the baseline model.

A full treatment of this population would require a two-dimensional screening problem over (θ,δk)(\theta,\delta_{k}), with vertical IC constraints in θ\theta and cross-state IC constraints between high- and low-sensitivity users. Here we isolate the degradation channel by comparing two baseline calculations, one for each sensitivity state, while holding the virtual type at 2​θ−12\theta-1. The correlation determines how the states are associated with consumer valuation; these calculations do not solve the resulting joint screening problem. For state k∈{L,H}k\in\{L,H\}, the diagnostic pointwise virtual surplus is

𝒱k​(θ,q,α)=(2​θ−1)​q​(1−δk​α)+λ​q​α+r¯​(α−α22)−q22.\mathcal{V}_{k}(\theta;q,\alpha)=(2\theta-1)q(1-\delta_{k}\alpha)+\lambda q\alpha+\bar{r}\left(\alpha-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\right)-\frac{q^{2}}{2}.

Thus the low-sensitivity benchmark exactly coincides with the baseline model, while the high-sensitivity benchmark is the same model with δ\delta replaced by 2​δ2\delta. This diagnostic has three implications.

  1. (a)(a)

    The δ\delta-driven non-monotonic quality-distortion mechanism continues to hold within each state-contingent benchmark: higher degradation weakly expands the positive-quality region, with strict expansion when its threshold moves within the type support; among positive-quality full-ad users, it raises quality below the median and lowers quality above it, preserves the heavy-ad/light-ad sign reversal in the interior region, and leaves ad-free quality unchanged.

  2. (b)(b)

    The r¯\bar{r}-driven allocation channel remains intact: higher baseline ad profitability increases interior ad load, lowers interior quality and effective quality, and preserves the rent-extraction force that raises prices for remaining ad-free premium users in the state-contingent benchmark.

  3. (c)(c)

    The utility-polarization comparison with pure subscription remains valid within each state-contingent benchmark. High-sensitivity users become more likely as θ\theta increases, but the statewise comparisons do not establish a utility ordering for an optimal mechanism in the joint correlated population.

These implications concern the two statewise calculations, including the indirect effect of lower-plan effective quality on ad-free users’ information rents. The supporting calculations are provided in Appendix D.16.

A.3 Positive Ad Utility

The baseline model treats embedded advertising as purely disruptive. We now allow ads to generate direct user value by reducing search costs or improving match quality. For instance, a high-quality model may embed a sponsored recommendation or booking link that improves the user’s match relative to unaided search. To capture this possibility, we augment user utility as

U⁡(θ)=θ​q​(1−δ​α)+η​q​α−T,U(\theta)=\theta q(1-\delta\alpha)+\eta q\alpha-T, (16)

where η≥0\eta\geq 0 captures the direct, type-independent matching value generated by advertising. The negative disruption term θ​q​δ​α\theta q\delta\alpha remains type-dependent because higher-value users suffer more from degraded analytical output, while the positive matching value η​q​α\eta q\alpha is type-independent.

Let λ~:=λ+η\tilde{\lambda}:=\lambda+\eta. To preserve the same ad-free premium structure as in the baseline model, we impose the following effective analogue of Assumption 3.7:

λ~∈(0,δ),r¯∈(0,δ−λ~).\tilde{\lambda}\in(0,\delta),\hskip 18.49988pt\bar{r}\in(0,\delta-\tilde{\lambda}).

Equivalently, the direct ad benefit must satisfy 0≤η<δ−λ−r¯0\leq\eta<\delta-\lambda-\bar{r}.

Proposition A.3 (Equivalence under Positive Ad Utility)

Under (16) and the effective regularity condition above, equilibrium thresholds, allocations, and consumer utilities coincide with those of the baseline model evaluated at λ~=λ+η\tilde{\lambda}=\lambda+\eta. Subscription payments satisfy

Tη​(θ)=Tbaseline​(θ,λ~)+η​q∗​(θ)​α∗​(θ).T_{\eta}(\theta)=T_{\mathrm{baseline}}(\theta;\tilde{\lambda})+\eta q^{*}(\theta)\alpha^{*}(\theta).

The allocation and utility results in Sections 4–5 therefore carry over after this substitution. The within-segment subscription-price responses to r¯\bar{r} in Proposition 5.2 also remain valid.

This result shows that positive ad utility does not overturn the baseline mechanism. Instead, it strengthens the effective advertising incentive: for a given allocation, the platform can extract the type-independent matching value through subscription payments without changing information rents. The proof is provided in Appendix D.17.

A.4 Type-Dependent Ad Monetization

In practice, the attention and inferred intent of high-valuation users may be more valuable for targeted advertising, B2B lead generation, or downstream conversion. To capture this, we allow the quality-driven ad premium to increase with the consumer’s vertical type: Λ⁡(θ)=λ+γ​θ\Lambda(\theta)=\lambda+\gamma\theta, where λ>0\lambda>0 is the baseline monetization rate and γ≥0\gamma\geq 0 captures the targeted premium. The pointwise virtual surplus becomes

𝒱γ​(θ,q,α)=(2​θ−1)​q​(1−δ​α)+(λ+γ​θ)​q​α+r¯​(α−α22)−q22.\mathcal{V}_{\gamma}(\theta;q,\alpha)=(2\theta-1)q(1-\delta\alpha)+(\lambda+\gamma\theta)q\alpha+\bar{r}\left(\alpha-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\right)-\frac{q^{2}}{2}. (17)

Let Δγ​(θ):=(2​θ−1)​δ−(λ+γ​θ)=(2​δ−γ)​θ−(δ+λ)\Delta_{\gamma}(\theta):=(2\theta-1)\delta-(\lambda+\gamma\theta)=(2\delta-\gamma)\theta-(\delta+\lambda). We impose 0≤γ<δ−λ−r¯0\leq\gamma<\delta-\lambda-\bar{r}. This restriction ensures Δγ​(1)>r¯\Delta_{\gamma}(1)>\bar{r} and therefore preserves an endogenous ad-free premium tier. The equilibrium thresholds are

θ¯γ=1−δ−λ2​(1−δ)+γ,θ1γ=δ+λ2​δ−γ,\underline{\theta}^{\gamma}=\frac{1-\delta-\lambda}{2(1-\delta)+\gamma},\hskip 18.49988pt\theta_{1}^{\gamma}=\frac{\delta+\lambda}{2\delta-\gamma},

and θ2γ\theta_{2}^{\gamma} is the unique solution to

(2​θ2γ−1)​Δγ​(θ2γ)=r¯.(2\theta_{2}^{\gamma}-1)\Delta_{\gamma}(\theta_{2}^{\gamma})=\bar{r}.

Interior allocations are obtained from the baseline formulas by replacing Δ⁡(θ)\Delta(\theta) with Δγ​(θ)\Delta_{\gamma}(\theta).

Proposition A.4 (Robustness under Type-Dependent Ad Monetization)

Under (17) and 0≤γ<δ−λ−r¯0\leq\gamma<\delta-\lambda-\bar{r}, the baseline equilibrium structure remains intact, with the following implications:

  1. (a)(a)

    Quality. Non-monotonic quality distortion with respect to δ\delta continues to hold.

  2. (b)(b)

    Prices. Higher baseline ad profitability r¯\bar{r} lowers interior effective quality and raises prices for users locally remaining ad-free. No global sign is asserted for interior prices under type-dependent ad monetization.

  3. (c)(c)

    Utility. The utility-polarization comparison with pure subscription continues to hold.

A higher premium for high-valuation consumers changes the thresholds, but the restriction on γ\gamma keeps advertising returns low enough at the top for an ad-free premium segment to remain. Within this region, low types remain ad-supported and intermediate types receive partial ad exposure. Higher baseline ad profitability still reduces effective quality in the interior, making those plans less attractive alternatives to ad-free service and allowing higher prices above. The type-dependent premium changes the variation in this effect across interior users, so the same allocation argument does not establish their price response. The proof is provided in Appendix D.18.

A.5 Concave Quality-Driven Advertising Premium

Our baseline analysis assumes that the quality-driven advertising premium is linear in response quality, taking the form λ​q​α\lambda q\alpha, so that higher response quality raises advertising value at a constant marginal rate. In practice, however, the marginal advertising value of quality may diminish: initial quality improvements can substantially improve intent inference and ad relevance, while further improvements may add less incremental advertising value. To examine the robustness of our main results, we extend the advertising revenue function to

Rh​(q,α)=λ​h​(q)​α+r¯​(α−α22),R_{h}(q,\alpha)=\lambda h(q)\alpha+\bar{r}\left(\alpha-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\right), (18)

where h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0, h′​(q)>0h^{\prime}(q)>0, h′′​(q)<0h^{\prime\prime}(q)<0 for q>0q>0, and h′​(0)<∞h^{\prime}(0)<\infty. The normalization h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0 means that the quality-driven premium vanishes at zero quality; baseline ad impressions at zero quality are still captured by r¯​(α−α2/2)\bar{r}(\alpha-\alpha^{2}/2). All other primitives remain as in the baseline model: g⁡(q,α)=q⁡(1−δ​α)g(q,\alpha)=q(1-\delta\alpha), cβ​(q)=β​q2/2c_{\beta}(q)=\beta q^{2}/2 with β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1], θ∼U⁡[0,1]\theta\sim U[0,1], and v⁡(θ)=2​θ−1v(\theta)=2\theta-1. We first set β=1\beta=1 to isolate robustness to concavity and characterize the resulting mechanism; after Proposition A.6, we restore β\beta to revisit the compute-efficiency result.

Setting β=1\beta=1, the pointwise virtual surplus under (18) is

𝒱h​(θ,q,α)=v⁡(θ)​q​(1−δ​α)+λ​h​(q)​α+r¯​(α−α22)−q22.\mathcal{V}_{h}(\theta;q,\alpha)=v(\theta)q(1-\delta\alpha)+\lambda h(q)\alpha+\bar{r}\left(\alpha-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\right)-\frac{q^{2}}{2}.

An interior solution satisfies q=v⁡(θ)​(1−δ​α)+λ​α​h′​(q)q=v(\theta)(1-\delta\alpha)+\lambda\alpha h^{\prime}(q) and δ​v​(θ)​q−λ​h​(q)=r¯​(1−α)\delta v(\theta)q-\lambda h(q)=\bar{r}(1-\alpha). Thus, relative to the baseline model, marginal quality provision is governed by h′​(q)h^{\prime}(q), while the boundary between ad-supported and ad-free service is governed by the average premium h⁡(q)/qh(q)/q.

Because a general concave function can generate multiple crossings, we impose the following regularity condition to preserve the same market region as in the baseline model.
