These are comparisons within the weighted-objective diagnostic, not predictions of list-price responses in a strategic platform market. The proofs are provided in Appendices D.22 and D.23.

Appendix B Assumptions and Supplementary Exhibits

B.1 Discussion of Assumptions

Functional Forms. Our analysis combines general structural results with a tractable closed-form baseline. The virtual-surplus decomposition (Lemma 4.1) and the virtual advertising profit (Definition 4.2) are derived under the general model; the explicit segment thresholds, closed-form allocations, and sharp comparative statics use the uniform-quadratic, multiplicative baseline. The multiplicative effective-quality form is economically substantive: a given ad load destroys more user value when more quality is supplied, linking output interference and privacy friction to the quality choice. The mixed-degradation extension adds a pure nuisance component while retaining this quality-related loss; it does not establish the same conclusions for purely additive nuisance. The extensions in Appendix A should therefore be read under their stated restrictions as scope diagnostics rather than as proof of functional-form invariance.

Consumer-Side Advertising Effects. We assume a single dimension of private information, θ\theta, which governs both the consumer’s valuation of AI quality and the utility loss from advertising-induced degradation. Under the baseline specification, g⁡(q,α)=q⁡(1−δ​α)g(q,\alpha)=q(1-\delta\alpha), advertising lowers the effective value of quality, so higher-type consumers suffer a greater absolute loss from a given ad load. In the LLM context, this captures that users who value high-quality, trustworthy outputs are also more exposed to output interference or privacy friction. The effects are not uniform: in a 179-participant chatbot experiment, Tang et al. (2025) find that users struggled to identify advertisements and sometimes preferred responses containing hidden advertising; their benchmark evaluations show only small changes in most performance measures. The baseline therefore focuses on settings in which advertising reduces effective user value.

Three extensions clarify the scope of this consumer-side specification. Appendix A.1 considers g⁡(q,α)=q⁡(1−δ​α)−δn​αg(q,\alpha)=q(1-\delta\alpha)-\delta_{n}\alpha, which separates the quality-related harm emphasized in LLM settings from a pure nuisance component more common in traditional media. Appendix A.2 allows ad sensitivity to covary with valuation by assuming that a type-θ\theta consumer faces the high-degradation state δH\delta_{H} with probability θ\theta and the low-degradation state δL\delta_{L} with probability 1−θ1-\theta, capturing the idea that higher-value users may be more sensitive to advertising-induced degradation. Appendix A.3 augments utility to U⁡(θ)=θ​q​(1−δ​α)+η​q​α−TU(\theta)=\theta q(1-\delta\alpha)+\eta q\alpha-T, allowing advertising to generate matching or informational value. These extensions delineate when the baseline mechanisms continue to operate under additional consumer-side advertising channels and where genuinely two-dimensional screening remains open. The ad-load screening and divergent-pricing results are derived under this maintained scalar-type structure. At a fixed quality and ad load, the term v⁡(θ)​(g⁡(q,0)−g⁡(q,α))=(2​θ−1)​q​δ​αv(\theta)\bigl(g(q,0)-g(q,\alpha)\bigr)=(2\theta-1)q\delta\alpha measures the reduction in virtual subscription value relative to ad-free service; it can be negative below the virtual-zero type. As θ\theta rises, a given ad load α\alpha becomes more costly in these virtual subscription terms. The correlated-degradation diagnostic (Appendix A.2) gives statewise comparisons while preserving the coupling between valuation and advertising sensitivity. A genuinely two-dimensional model with independent or negatively correlated preferences for quality and advertising avoidance remains open; the existing diagnostics do not establish the same α\alpha-schedule or four-segment structure in that setting.

Platform-Side Advertising Revenue. In the baseline, advertising revenue depends on endogenous response quality, R⁡(q,α)R(q,\alpha), rather than directly on the consumer’s type. Because the platform assigns different quality levels q∗​(θ)q^{*}(\theta) across segments, ad monetization becomes endogenously type-dependent. This captures the possibility that richer responses reveal more commercial intent and increase advertising value. Appendix A.4 also allows a directly type-dependent premium, with R⁡(q,α,θ)=(λ+γ​θ)​q​α+r¯​(α−α2/2)R(q,\alpha;\theta)=(\lambda+\gamma\theta)q\alpha+\bar{r}(\alpha-\alpha^{2}/2) and γ≥0\gamma\geq 0. Appendix A.5 instead allows diminishing marginal returns to quality, with R⁡(q,α)=λ​h​(q)​α+r¯​(α−α2/2)R(q,\alpha)=\lambda h(q)\alpha+\bar{r}(\alpha-\alpha^{2}/2), where h′​(q)>0h^{\prime}(q)>0 and h′′​(q)<0h^{\prime\prime}(q)<0. Under their respective restrictions, these extensions identify which baseline mechanisms survive direct type dependence or a concave quality-driven premium.

Commitment. We assume that the platform can commit to the posted menu of quality, advertising intensity, and prices, as is standard in screening models and broadly consistent with subscription markets where plan attributes and ad policies are disclosed ex ante. This full-commitment assumption is what licenses the revelation-principle reduction used in Section 4 and the binding-IR, envelope-transfer construction in Lemma 4.1. The assumption is substantive in the LLM context because sponsored responses and data-driven targeting may be difficult for users to fully monitor. We therefore view the model as a full-commitment benchmark that isolates the allocative logic of hybrid monetization. If commitment were imperfect, the direction of the welfare effect is not obvious: ex post ad expansion would impose an additional trust constraint that plausibly deepens the losses of partial-ad and ad-free users, but reputational discipline or the unraveling of credible ad-free tiers could instead force the platform to concede additional rents. We accordingly view the no-commitment mechanism-design problem as open rather than conjecture its resolution.

Market Structure. The monopoly baseline isolates how a single platform designs its menu; its welfare results depend on the information rents left to consumers, including the high-type utility losses in Proposition 5.3. Appendix A.6 examines this boundary through a reduced-form rent pass-through diagnostic in the spirit of conduct-parameter and pass-through approaches (Armstrong and Vickers 2001, Mahoney and Weyl 2017, Weyl and Fabinger 2013): a parameter κ∈[0,1]\kappa\in[0,1] scales down the monopoly screening wedge, with κ=0\kappa=0 recovering the monopoly benchmark and κ=1\kappa=1 the efficient endpoint. The ordering of the advertising regimes and the local divergent-pricing mechanism survive for every κ\kappa, allowing a zero-quality segment to be empty. The stronger claim that all full-ad low types gain holds if and only if κ≤1−λ/(1−δ)\kappa\leq 1-\lambda/(1-\delta) (Proposition A.9). The diagnostic captures rent pass-through, not strategic interaction: business stealing, multi-homing, and competitive discipline on ad loads remain outside the model. It therefore preserves a conditional cross-tier comparison—a marginal increase in baseline ad profitability lowers prices for users remaining partially ad-supported and raises prices for users remaining ad-free—without establishing the price levels or advertising policies of competing platforms.

Scope and Specificity. Ultimately, while the paper is motivated by generative AI, our framework should be interpreted as a broader theory of ad-supported digital platforms with endogenous quality provision, with LLM platforms serving as a leading application. The LLM setting is particularly suited to this framework because it combines three forces that are typically studied separately. First, quality is not a fixed content attribute: platforms can adjust model capability, inference depth, context length, and usage limits across user segments, all at increasing computational cost. Second, advertising can interfere with the core user experience through output interference or privacy friction, rather than merely consuming peripheral attention. Third, richer interactions can increase advertising value by revealing more precise commercial intent. We do not claim that hybrid monetization is exclusive to LLMs. Rather, the analysis identifies how the interplay of endogenous quality, ad-induced degradation, and quality-driven ad value shapes pricing, coverage, welfare, and tier design.

Remark B.1 clarifies how strict convexity shapes the form of quality adjustment underlying the baseline result.

Remark B.1 (Role of Convex Quality Costs)

Strict convexity supports the smooth, type-dependent quality adjustments underlying the baseline characterization of Proposition 5.3, but it is not necessary for utility polarization itself. If quality were costless and unconstrained, the platform’s pointwise virtual surplus 𝒱⁡(θ,q,α)\mathcal{V}(\theta;q,\alpha) would be unbounded in qq for any type with a positive marginal virtual benefit; with an independently fixed finite technological ceiling, the platform would instead choose maximum feasible quality whenever this marginal benefit is positive. More generally, under linear costs (c⁡(q)=μ​qc(q)=\mu q), quality becomes a threshold decision: provide maximum feasible quality if the marginal virtual benefit exceeds μ\mu, and zero otherwise. Linear costs therefore replace the baseline’s smooth, type-dependent quality adjustments with boundary choices. Advertising and information-rent effects can nevertheless still generate utility polarization, so strict convexity shapes the form of the baseline allocation rather than serving as a necessary condition for the polarization result.

Figure 5 illustrates the allocation mechanism behind the interior-cap optimum of Proposition 6.1 at the stated parameters. Relative to the unregulated menu, the interior cap raises effective quality for many low types, while a complete ban leaves the bottom without positive quality. For the ad-free top, effective quality coincides under the interior cap and the unregulated menu, yet utility differs because changes in lower plans alter the information rents left to higher types.

Table 3 reports the exact tier phase transitions underlying Proposition 7.1.

Appendix C Additional Equilibrium and Welfare Results

This appendix examines three departures or comparisons beyond the baseline characterization: equilibrium outside the regular parameter region, the local social-welfare effect of advertising caps, and the optimal mechanism under lower compute costs.

C.1 Equilibrium Structure under Extended Parameter Spaces

The baseline Market Regularity condition (Assumption 3.7) imposes λ<δ\lambda<\delta and r¯<δ−λ\bar{r}<\delta-\lambda to sustain an endogenous ad-free high-type segment. Under the normalized baseline ceiling q¯=1\bar{q}=1, these restrictions also avoid a positive-measure quality-constrained segment. We now relax these advertising-return bounds to examine larger quality-driven ad premiums or baseline impression profitability, while maintaining 0<δ<10<\delta<1. Stronger advertising returns can make advertising profitable even for high types, eliminating the positive-measure ad-free segment. When the quality-driven premium is sufficiently large, the added advertising return to quality can also push the optimum to the upper bound q¯=1\bar{q}=1. Table 4 characterizes the resulting regimes; the discussion below then distinguishes local allocation and price responses from the utility comparison with pure subscription.

Quality Responses to Ad Degradation (δ\delta). Under Assumption 3.7, Proposition 5.1 leaves users who remain ad-free at their pure-subscription monopoly quality. Outside that region (where r¯≥δ−λ\bar{r}\geq\delta-\lambda or λ\lambda is sufficiently large), the positive-measure ad-free segment disappears, and quality responses depend on both ad intensity and the technological ceiling. For below-median full-ad users, greater degradation makes their plans less attractive to higher types and lowers the screening cost of quality provision. Provided quality is positive and remains below the ceiling, the platform therefore raises supplied quality, so ∂q∗/∂δ>0\partial q^{*}/\partial\delta>0; zero-quality types remain at q∗=0q^{*}=0 unless a moving threshold brings them into positive quality. For types θ>1/2\theta>1/2 who remain fully advertised below the ceiling in Regimes 2 and 4, greater degradation lowers the virtual return to quality, giving ∂q∗∂δ<0\frac{\partial q^{*}}{\partial\delta}<0. For any type whose upper quality bound remains binding, quality is unchanged (q∗=1q^{*}=1, yielding ∂q∗∂δ=0\frac{\partial q^{*}}{\partial\delta}=0). Within the partial-ad segments of Regimes 1 and 3, the baseline heavy-ad/light-ad sign reversal remains, but there is no positive-measure ad-free endpoint.

Price Responses to Baseline Advertising Profitability (r¯\bar{r}). Proposition 5.2 establishes that a marginal increase in baseline ad profitability lowers prices for users remaining partially ad-supported and raises prices for users remaining ad-free. The latter segment loses positive measure at r¯=δ−λ\bar{r}=\delta-\lambda. When r¯≥δ−λ\bar{r}\geq\delta-\lambda in Regimes 1 and 3, types θ>θ1\theta>\theta_{1} receive the interior allocation; their ad loads satisfy αi​n​t>0\alpha^{int}>0 except that the highest type remains ad-free at equality. For users who remain in the partial-ad segment, a marginal increase in r¯\bar{r} lowers prices as their effective quality declines. The upper-tier price-increase mechanism has no positive-measure ad-free segment on which to operate. Prices for zero-quality and full-ad low types remain locally unaffected by r¯\bar{r}, because their ad load stays at the upper bound α∗=1\alpha^{*}=1.

Utility Comparisons outside the Regular Region (λ\lambda). Within the regular region, Proposition 5.3 shows that some fully ad-supported low types gain relative to pure subscription, while partially ad-supported and ad-free users strictly lose. Outside that region, positive advertising exposure alone does not determine the utility comparison. When λ≥δ\lambda\geq\delta (Regimes 2 and 4), the marginal virtual return to advertising is nonnegative for every type, so α∗​(θ)=1\alpha^{*}(\theta)=1 and

q∗​(θ)=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,(1−δ)​(2​θ−1)+λ}},Ua​d​(θ)=(1−δ)​∫0θq∗​(t)​𝑑t.q^{*}(\theta)=\min\{1,\max\{0,(1-\delta)(2\theta-1)+\lambda\}\},\hskip 18.49988ptU^{ad}(\theta)=(1-\delta)\int_{0}^{\theta}q^{*}(t)\,dt.

At universal pooling, which occurs when λ≥2−δ\lambda\geq 2-\delta, utility becomes Ua​d​(θ)=(1−δ)​θU^{ad}(\theta)=(1-\delta)\theta and the highest-type difference is 3/4−δ3/4-\delta. Every positive type then gains when δ<3/4\delta<3/4; the highest type is indifferent at δ=3/4\delta=3/4, while an upper interval loses when δ>3/4\delta>3/4. C.2 Advertising Caps and Social Welfare

Returning to the baseline specification under Assumption 3.7, we examine how the advertising-cap mechanism in Section 6.1 affects social welfare, defined as consumer surplus plus platform profit. This comparison is more demanding than the consumer-surplus comparison: although a cap can reduce advertising-induced degradation and benefit consumers, a binding cap restricts the platform’s feasible choice set and reduces its optimal profit. A cap therefore raises social welfare only when the consumer-surplus gain exceeds the profit loss.

Corollary C.1

A marginal tightening of the unregulated advertising level can raise social welfare only under extreme ad-induced degradation. In particular, such a local social-welfare gain requires

δ>1+2​24≈0.957.\delta>\frac{1+2\sqrt{2}}{4}\approx 0.957.

When this condition holds, the gain occurs for the intermediate interval of the quality-driven ad premium characterized in the proof.

Corollary C.1 identifies a narrow local possibility. For δ≤(1+2​2)/4\delta\leq(1+2\sqrt{2})/4, marginally tightening the unregulated benchmark cannot raise social welfare through the mechanism analyzed here. Only at higher degradation, and for the intermediate premium interval specified in the proof, can the gain from improved effective quality and reduced screening distortion exceed the platform’s lost profit. This comparison concerns a sufficiently small tightening from the unregulated benchmark; it does not characterize the globally optimal cap or imply that a larger tightening also improves welfare.

C.3 Equilibrium under Compute Efficiency

This subsection maintains Assumption 3.7, relaxes the baseline normalization β=1\beta=1, and characterizes the optimal mechanism for β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1]. The cost function is c⁡(q)=β​q22c(q)=\frac{\beta q^{2}}{2}, so a lower β\beta reduces the marginal cost of delivering quality. We hold the other primitives fixed: θ∼U⁡[0,1]\theta\sim U[0,1], g⁡(q,α)=q⁡(1−δ​α)g(q,\alpha)=q(1-\delta\alpha), and R⁡(q,α)=λ​q​α+r¯​(α−α22)R(q,\alpha)=\lambda q\alpha+\bar{r}\left(\alpha-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\right). We maintain the technological-ceiling convention c′​(q¯)=1c^{\prime}(\bar{q})=1, which implies q¯=1/β\bar{q}=1/\beta; the ceiling therefore expands as compute becomes more efficient, so the allocations characterized below lie within the feasible quality range. Let v⁡(θ):=2​θ−1v(\theta):=2\theta-1 and Δ⁡(θ):=v⁡(θ)​δ−λ\Delta(\theta):=v(\theta)\delta-\lambda. The pointwise virtual surplus is

𝒱β​(θ,q,α)=v⁡(θ)​q​(1−δ​α)+λ​q​α+r¯​(α−α22)−β​q22.\mathcal{V}_{\beta}(\theta;q,\alpha)=v(\theta)q(1-\delta\alpha)+\lambda q\alpha+\bar{r}\left(\alpha-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\right)-\frac{\beta q^{2}}{2}. (21)

For a fixed ad load α\alpha, the first-order condition with respect to quality yields

qβ∗​(θ,α)=max⁡{0,v⁡(θ)​(1−δ​α)+λ​αβ}.q_{\beta}^{*}(\theta,\alpha)=\max\left\{0,\frac{v(\theta)(1-\delta\alpha)+\lambda\alpha}{\beta}\right\}.

The marginal virtual surplus with respect to advertising is

∂𝒱β∂α=−Δ⁡(θ)​q+r¯​(1−α).\frac{\partial\mathcal{V}_{\beta}}{\partial\alpha}=-\Delta(\theta)q+\bar{r}(1-\alpha).

We first define the relevant thresholds.

Definition C.2 (Thresholds under Compute Efficiency)

Define the following thresholds:

  1. (a)(a)

    Positive-quality threshold: θ¯:=12−λ2​(1−δ)\underline{\theta}:=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{2(1-\delta)}, above which the platform provides strictly positive quality.

  2. (b)(b)

    Partial-ad threshold: θ1:=12+λ2​δ\theta_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2\delta}, above which the platform transitions to a partial ad load.

  3. (c)(c)

    Ad-free threshold: θ2,β∈(θ1,1]\theta_{2,\beta}\in(\theta_{1},1] uniquely solving (2​θ2,β−1)​((2​θ2,β−1)​δ−λ)=β​r¯(2\theta_{2,\beta}-1)\big((2\theta_{2,\beta}-1)\delta-\lambda\big)=\beta\bar{r}, or equivalently, θ2,β=2​δ+λ+λ2+4​δ​β​r¯4​δ\theta_{2,\beta}=\frac{2\delta+\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+4\delta\beta\bar{r}}}{4\delta}.

The first two thresholds are unchanged relative to the baseline model, while the ad-free threshold shifts with β\beta. We now characterize the optimal mechanism.

Theorem C.3 (Optimal Mechanism under Compute Efficiency)

The optimal mechanism takes the following form:

  1. (a)(a)

    Zero-quality types (θ∈[0,θ¯]\theta\in[0,\underline{\theta}], empty when θ¯<0\underline{\theta}<0): qβ∗​(θ)=0q_{\beta}^{*}(\theta)=0, αβ∗​(θ)=1\alpha_{\beta}^{*}(\theta)=1, and Tβ∗​(θ)=0T_{\beta}^{*}(\theta)=0.

  2. (b)(b)

    Low types (θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1] with θ¯<θ≤θ1\underline{\theta}<\theta\leq\theta_{1}): αβ∗​(θ)=1\alpha_{\beta}^{*}(\theta)=1 and qβ∗​(θ)=(2​θ−1)​(1−δ)+λβ>0q_{\beta}^{*}(\theta)=\frac{(2\theta-1)(1-\delta)+\lambda}{\beta}>0. The payment at θ=0\theta=0 is Tβ∗​(0)=0T_{\beta}^{*}(0)=0 when θ¯<0\underline{\theta}<0.

  3. (c)(c)

    Medium types (θ∈(θ1,θ2,β)\theta\in(\theta_{1},\theta_{2,\beta})):

    αβi​n​t​(θ):=β​r¯−(2​θ−1)​((2​θ−1)​δ−λ)β​r¯−((2​θ−1)​δ−λ)2,qβi​n​t​(θ):=r¯​[λ+(2​θ−1)​(1−δ)]β​r¯−((2​θ−1)​δ−λ)2.\alpha_{\beta}^{int}(\theta):=\frac{\beta\bar{r}-(2\theta-1)\big((2\theta-1)\delta-\lambda\big)}{\beta\bar{r}-\big((2\theta-1)\delta-\lambda\big)^{2}},\hskip 18.49988ptq_{\beta}^{int}(\theta):=\frac{\bar{r}\big[\lambda+(2\theta-1)(1-\delta)\big]}{\beta\bar{r}-\big((2\theta-1)\delta-\lambda\big)^{2}}.
  4. (d)(d)

    High types (θ∈[θ2,β,1]\theta\in[\theta_{2,\beta},1]): αβ∗​(θ)=0\alpha_{\beta}^{*}(\theta)=0 and qβ∗​(θ)=2​θ−1βq_{\beta}^{*}(\theta)=\frac{2\theta-1}{\beta}.

Moreover, the effective quality g⁡(qβ∗​(θ),αβ∗​(θ))g(q_{\beta}^{*}(\theta),\alpha_{\beta}^{*}(\theta)) remains non-decreasing in θ\theta.

Theorem C.3 preserves the baseline ordering of advertising regimes; subscription payments are recovered from (9). A lower β\beta raises positive quality by making it cheaper to supply. For users who remain partially advertised, higher quality increases the net virtual cost of advertising-induced degradation, so the platform reduces ad intensity. Once even the first increment of advertising is no longer profitable, a plan becomes ad-free; accordingly, the threshold θ2,β\theta_{2,\beta} falls and the ad-free segment expands. The condition for a zero-quality segment is unchanged because θ¯=1/2−λ/[2​(1−δ)]\underline{\theta}=1/2-\lambda/[2(1-\delta)] does not depend on β\beta. That segment has positive measure if λ<1−δ\lambda<1-\delta, consists only of θ=0\theta=0 if λ=1−δ\lambda=1-\delta, and is empty if λ>1−δ\lambda>1-\delta. The proof is provided in Appendix D.10.

Appendix D Proofs

We first derive the virtual-surplus representation, solve the pointwise allocation problem, and verify that the resulting menu is incentive compatible. The subsequent proofs establish the quality, price, utility, and welfare comparisons, followed by the compute-efficiency and discrete-tier results. Further proofs cover the model extensions. Each proof maintains the assumptions stated for its result.

Proof: The optimal subscription price is T∗​(θ)=θ​g​(q∗​(θ),α∗​(θ))−U⁡(θ)T^{*}(\theta)=\theta g(q^{*}(\theta),\alpha^{*}(\theta))-U(\theta), where U⁡(θ)=∫0θg⁡(q∗​(t),α∗​(t))​𝑑tU(\theta)=\int_{0}^{\theta}g(q^{*}(t),\alpha^{*}(t))\,dt is the information rent. Part (a): Zero-quality and low types (θ≤θ1\theta\leq\theta_{1}). For these fully ad-supported users, α∗=1\alpha^{*}=1 and q∗​(θ)=max⁡{0,(2​θ−1)​(1−δ)+λ}q^{*}(\theta)=\max\{0,(2\theta-1)(1-\delta)+\lambda\}, both of which are independent of r¯\bar{r}. On (θ1,θ2)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) we have Δ⁡(θ)>0\Delta(\theta)>0, Δ⁡(θ)−s<0\Delta(\theta)-s<0, and r¯−Δ​(θ)2>0\bar{r}-\Delta(\theta)^{2}>0; moreover C⁡(θ)C(\theta) is increasing in ss with minimum value λ>0\lambda>0 attained at s=λ/δs=\lambda/\delta, so the bracket is strictly positive. Hence χ⁡(θ)<0\chi(\theta)<0 strictly on the open interval, with χ⁡(θ1)=0\chi(\theta_{1})=0 (the factor Δ⁡(θ1)=0\Delta(\theta_{1})=0). To establish monotonicity, set x:=Δ⁡(θ)=δ​s−λx:=\Delta(\theta)=\delta s-\lambda. Then s=(x+λ)/δs=(x+\lambda)/\delta, C⁡(θ)=λ+2​(1−δ)​xC(\theta)=\lambda+2(1-\delta)x, and Δ(θ)−s=−[(1−δ)x+λ]/δ\Delta(\theta)-s=-[(1-\delta)x+\lambda]/\delta, so

−χ⁡(θ)=x⁡[(1−δ)​x+λ]​{r¯​[λ+2​(1−δ)​x]+λ​x2}δ​(r¯−x2)3.-\chi(\theta)=\frac{x\bigl[(1-\delta)x+\lambda\bigr]\bigl\{\bar{r}[\lambda+2(1-\delta)x]+\lambda x^{2}\bigr\}}{\delta(\bar{r}-x^{2})^{3}}.

On the interior segment, x>0x>0 and r¯−x2>0\bar{r}-x^{2}>0. Every numerator factor is positive and weakly increasing (the leading factor strictly), whereas the positive denominator decreases. Thus higher r¯\bar{r} lowers interior effective quality, increasingly so for higher medium types.

Using T∗​(θ)=θ​g∗​(θ)−U⁡(θ)T^{*}(\theta)=\theta g^{*}(\theta)-U(\theta) and U⁡(θ)=∫0θg∗​(t)​𝑑tU(\theta)=\int_{0}^{\theta}g^{*}(t)dt, and noting that allocations below θ1\theta_{1} are independent of r¯\bar{r}, we obtain

∂T∗​(θ)∂r¯<θ​χ​(θ)−(θ−θ1)​χ​(θ)=θ1​χ​(θ)<0.\frac{\partial T^{*}(\theta)}{\partial\bar{r}}<\theta\chi(\theta)-(\theta-\theta_{1})\chi(\theta)=\theta_{1}\chi(\theta)<0.

Therefore, medium-type prices strictly decrease with r¯\bar{r}.

Part (c): High types (θ≥θ2\theta\geq\theta_{2}). The ad-free threshold satisfies

θ2=2​δ+λ+λ2+4​δ​r¯4​δ,∂θ2∂r¯=12​λ2+4​δ​r¯>0.\theta_{2}=\frac{2\delta+\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+4\delta\bar{r}}}{4\delta},\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\partial\theta_{2}}{\partial\bar{r}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+4\delta\bar{r}}}>0.

Thus, a higher r¯\bar{r} shifts the ad-free threshold rightward. The price comparison below applies to users who remain above that moving threshold.

Users remaining ad-free. Users remaining ad-free keep (α∗,q∗)=(0,2​θ−1)(\alpha^{*},q^{*})=(0,2\theta-1), so ∂g∗​(θ)/∂r¯=0\partial g^{*}(\theta)/\partial\bar{r}=0, but their information rent falls because medium-type effective quality falls:

D.8 Proof of Proposition 6.1

Proof D.8

Proof: Let C​S​(α¯,δ,λ,r¯)CS(\bar{\alpha};\delta,\lambda,\bar{r}) denote aggregate consumer surplus under the advertising cap α⁡(θ)≤α¯\alpha(\theta)\leq\bar{\alpha}. By the envelope condition, C​S​(α¯,δ,λ,r¯)=∫01(1−θ)​g∗​(θ,α¯)​𝑑θCS(\bar{\alpha};\delta,\lambda,\bar{r})=\int_{0}^{1}(1-\theta)g^{*}(\theta;\bar{\alpha})\,d\theta. Continuity of the constrained pointwise problem and compactness imply that C​SCS is continuous on [0,1][0,1] and admits a maximizer. We first derive the local effect at the unregulated cap, then separately establish a nonempty region in which every maximizing cap is interior.

Because tightening means lowering α¯\bar{\alpha}, a negative left derivative at α¯=1\bar{\alpha}=1 implies a local consumer-surplus gain. Only positive-quality fully advertised types contribute to this first-order effect. Their constrained effective quality is g∗​(θ,α¯)=[(2​θ−1)​(1−δ​α¯)+λ​α¯]​(1−δ​α¯)g^{*}(\theta;\bar{\alpha})=[(2\theta-1)(1-\delta\bar{\alpha})+\lambda\bar{\alpha}](1-\delta\bar{\alpha}), so the left derivative is

Φ⁡(δ,λ):=d​C​Sd​α¯|α¯=1=∫max⁡{0,θ¯}θ1(1−θ)​[−2​δ​(1−δ)​(2​θ−1)+λ⁡(1−2​δ)]​𝑑θ.\Phi(\delta,\lambda):=\left.\frac{dCS}{d\bar{\alpha}}\right|_{\bar{\alpha}=1}=\int_{\max\{0,\underline{\theta}\}}^{\theta_{1}}(1-\theta)\left[-2\delta(1-\delta)(2\theta-1)+\lambda(1-2\delta)\right]d\theta.

If λ<1−δ\lambda<1-\delta, then θ¯>0\underline{\theta}>0 and the saturated positive-quality region is [θ¯,θ1][\underline{\theta},\theta_{1}], giving

Φ⁡(δ,λ)=∫θ¯θ1(1−θ)​[−2​δ​(1−δ)​(2​θ−1)+λ⁡(1−2​δ)]​𝑑θ=λ324​δ2​(1−δ)2>0.\Phi(\delta,\lambda)=\int_{\underline{\theta}}^{\theta_{1}}(1-\theta)\left[-2\delta(1-\delta)(2\theta-1)+\lambda(1-2\delta)\right]d\theta=\frac{\lambda^{3}}{24\delta^{2}(1-\delta)^{2}}>0.

Thus marginal tightening reduces consumer surplus in this region.

If λ≥1−δ\lambda\geq 1-\delta, then θ¯≤0\underline{\theta}\leq 0 and the saturated region starts at zero, yielding

Φ⁡(δ,λ)\displaystyle\Phi(\delta,\lambda) =∫0θ1(1−θ)​[−2​δ​(1−δ)​(2​θ−1)+λ⁡(1−2​δ)]​𝑑θ\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\theta_{1}}(1-\theta)\left[-2\delta(1-\delta)(2\theta-1)+\lambda(1-2\delta)\right]\,d\theta
=δ+λ24​δ2​[(2​δ+1)​λ2−δ⁡(8​δ+1)​λ+10​δ2​(1−δ)].\displaystyle=\frac{\delta+\lambda}{24\delta^{2}}\left[(2\delta+1)\lambda^{2}-\delta(8\delta+1)\lambda+10\delta^{2}(1-\delta)\right].

Since (δ+λ)/(24​δ2)>0(\delta+\lambda)/(24\delta^{2})>0, we have Φ⁡(δ,λ)<0\Phi(\delta,\lambda)<0 if and only if

(2​δ+1)​λ2−δ⁡(8​δ+1)​λ+10​δ2​(1−δ)<0.(2\delta+1)\lambda^{2}-\delta(8\delta+1)\lambda+10\delta^{2}(1-\delta)<0.

Hence, when δ>5/8\delta>5/8, marginally tightening the unregulated cap strictly increases consumer surplus whenever

λ>λ^local​(δ):=δ⁡[(8​δ+1)−144​δ2−24​δ−39]2​(2​δ+1).\lambda>\hat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{local}}(\delta):=\frac{\delta\left[(8\delta+1)-\sqrt{144\delta^{2}-24\delta-39}\right]}{2(2\delta+1)}.

Under this condition, Φ⁡(δ,λ)<0\Phi(\delta,\lambda)<0, so lowering α¯\bar{\alpha} slightly raises consumer surplus and α¯=1\bar{\alpha}=1 cannot maximize it.

To establish interior optimality for a nonempty set of primitives, we now compare a feasible interior cap with both endpoints. Under a total ad ban, α¯=0\bar{\alpha}=0, the model collapses to the pure-subscription monopoly, so

C​S​(0,δ,λ,r¯)=∫1/21(1−θ)​(2​θ−1)​𝑑θ=124.CS(0;\delta,\lambda,\bar{r})=\int_{1/2}^{1}(1-\theta)(2\theta-1)\,d\theta=\frac{1}{24}.

For (δ,λ,r¯)=(0.9,0.5,0.18)(\delta,\lambda,\bar{r})=(0.9,0.5,0.18), the local condition holds, and direct integration of the globally optimal pointwise allocation yields

C​S​(0.78)≈0.04898,C​S​(0)≈0.04167,C​S​(1)≈0.03155.CS(0.78)\approx 0.04898,\hskip 18.49988ptCS(0)\approx 0.04167,\hskip 18.49988ptCS(1)\approx 0.03155.

The feasible cap 0.780.78 strictly dominates both endpoints; it need not be the maximizing cap. Since a maximizer exists, every maximizer at this instance must therefore be interior. Strictness of the comparisons and continuity in the primitives extend the conclusion to a neighborhood of this instance. □\square

D.9 Proof of Corollary C.1

Proof D.9

Proof: Let S​W​(α¯,δ,λ,r¯):=C​S​(α¯,δ,λ,r¯)+Π⁡(α¯,δ,λ,r¯)SW(\bar{\alpha};\delta,\lambda,\bar{r}):=CS(\bar{\alpha};\delta,\lambda,\bar{r})+\Pi(\bar{\alpha};\delta,\lambda,\bar{r}) denote aggregate social welfare under the cap α⁡(θ)≤α¯\alpha(\theta)\leq\bar{\alpha}. Since the constrained allocation varies continuously with α¯\bar{\alpha} over the compact interval [0,1][0,1], S​W​(α¯,δ,λ,r¯)SW(\bar{\alpha};\delta,\lambda,\bar{r}) is continuous and admits a maximizer.

We characterize when marginal tightening from α¯=1\bar{\alpha}=1 increases welfare. Only fully advertised types contribute to the first-order effect, and zero-quality types have no first-order welfare contribution at this boundary. Write x:=2​θ−1x:=2\theta-1. For a positive-quality type at the full ad load, q∗​(x,1)=x⁡(1−δ)+λq^{*}(x,1)=x(1-\delta)+\lambda. We first derive its marginal contribution, then integrate over the relevant positive-quality segment.

Since ∂g/∂α|α=1=λ⁡(1−2​δ)−2​x​δ​(1−δ)\partial g/\partial\alpha|_{\alpha=1}=\lambda(1-2\delta)-2x\delta(1-\delta), the corresponding contribution is Mc​s​(x)=1−x2​[λ⁡(1−2​δ)−2​x​δ​(1−δ)]M_{cs}(x)=\frac{1-x}{2}[\lambda(1-2\delta)-2x\delta(1-\delta)]. If 0<λ≤1−δ0<\lambda\leq 1-\delta, the closure of the positive-quality fully advertised segment is x∈[−λ/(1−δ),λ/δ]x\in[-\lambda/(1-\delta),\lambda/\delta]. Using d​θ=d​x/2d\theta=dx/2 gives

d​S​Wd​α¯|α¯=1=12∫−λ/(1−δ)λ/δMs​w(x)dx=λ38​δ2​(1−δ)2>0.\left.\frac{dSW}{d\bar{\alpha}}\right|_{\bar{\alpha}=1}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\lambda/(1-\delta)}^{\lambda/\delta}M_{sw}(x)\,dx=\frac{\lambda^{3}}{8\delta^{2}(1-\delta)^{2}}>0.

Thus marginal tightening reduces welfare throughout this branch, including λ=1−δ\lambda=1-\delta.

If λ>1−δ\lambda>1-\delta, all fully advertised types receive positive quality and the relevant interval is x∈[−1,λ/δ]x\in[-1,\lambda/\delta]. Integrating over this interval yields

(2+1δ)​λ2−λ+2​δ​(1−δ)<0.\left(2+\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\lambda^{2}-\lambda+2\delta(1-\delta)<0.

Its solution interval is nonempty exactly when 16​δ2−8​δ−7>016\delta^{2}-8\delta-7>0, or δ>(1+2​2)/4\delta>(1+2\sqrt{2})/4. Thus no λ\lambda supports a local welfare gain when δ≤(1+2​2)/4\delta\leq(1+2\sqrt{2})/4; the possibility is confined to extreme degradation. For such δ\delta, define the local interval

λ¯s​wloc​(δ)=δ⁡[1−16​δ2−8​δ−7]2​(2​δ+1),λ¯s​wloc​(δ)=δ⁡[1+16​δ2−8​δ−7]2​(2​δ+1).\underline{\lambda}_{sw}^{\mathrm{loc}}(\delta)=\frac{\delta\left[1-\sqrt{16\delta^{2}-8\delta-7}\right]}{2(2\delta+1)},\hskip 18.49988pt\overline{\lambda}_{sw}^{\mathrm{loc}}(\delta)=\frac{\delta\left[1+\sqrt{16\delta^{2}-8\delta-7}\right]}{2(2\delta+1)}.

Hence full-ad quality rises for θ<1/2\theta<1/2 and falls for θ>1/2\theta>1/2 in both states. The cutoff θ¯k=1/2−λ/[2​(1−δk)]\underline{\theta}_{k}=1/2-\lambda/[2(1-\delta_{k})] shifts leftward. In the interior region, Proposition 5.1’s implicit-function argument gives

For baseline ad profitability, differentiating the interior formulas yields ∂qki​n​t/∂r¯<0\partial q_{k}^{int}/\partial\bar{r}<0 and ∂αki​n​t/∂r¯>0\partial\alpha_{k}^{int}/\partial\bar{r}>0 in the interior region. Since gk​(q,α)=q⁡(1−δk​α)g_{k}(q,\alpha)=q(1-\delta_{k}\alpha) and δk<1\delta_{k}<1, interior effective quality falls with r¯\bar{r}. Thus the allocation channel behind Proposition 5.2 is preserved in each state-contingent benchmark. Finally, since δL=δ\delta_{L}=\delta and δH=2​δ\delta_{H}=2\delta both satisfy the analogue of Assumption 3.7, Proposition 5.3 applies separately to both state-contingent benchmarks.
